https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c804: Rohingya genocide: What was said in court and what happens now?
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.

A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
Rohingyas at the Cox's Bazar camp in Bangladesh, where around a million refugees now reside, watched the verdict live
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.

Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.

The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Watch: Genocide judgement will 'mean a great deal' for Rohingya community

Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.

Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.

While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.

In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.

The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c623: Watch: What did Trump, Xi and Putin get out of their historic meeting?
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.
The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.

In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.

Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".
Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.
In the same post, the president announced he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.
While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".
He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".
Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.
Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.
Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".
Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.

China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.
Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.
Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.
"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."
Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".
It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."
Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.
He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".
Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".

He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckzd: European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

US President Donald Trump's envoys were also there, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner said Trump wanted to make a deal with Russia "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition. Russia has never accepted the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but Article Five-style guarantees could theoretically be offered to Kyiv without being part of the Western defensive alliance.

Zelensky and the three European leaders - Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron - were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, Witkoff and Kushner appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.

But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c58j: Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat said to be carrying between 50 and 100 migrants capsized in the Atlantic Ocean.
Four bodies have reportedly been recovered so far. Dozens of people are still missing.

Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.
This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.
Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).
"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.
A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.
However, a local official told Reuters news agency it was carrying 50 people, adding that the boat hit a rock as migrants were transferring from small fishing boats to a larger vessel.
Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.
At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.
He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.
Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.
Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.
The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.
It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.
The Senegalese navy said it had rescued more than 1,400 people on Monday and Tuesday this week.

As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.
They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.
Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.
They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.
On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.
It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm87: Vladimir Putin spoke at a press conference following a historic summit with Xi Jinping and Donald Trump
Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed.
In the early hours of Thursday, the double-arched, 12-mile bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea was hit for a third time this week.
A combined missile-and-drone strike on Tuesday destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it into the water and rendering it unusable for road traffic.
But at a press conference after historic talks with his Chinese and US counterparts in Shenzhen, Russian president Putin said Moscow's response would be even more significant.
Putin claimed the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged, or petroleum products.
Since illegally annexing the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, Moscow has used it as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles.
From there it has also carried out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplied its troops in southern Ukraine.

Commenting on the strikes on the bridge, Kyiv's defence ministry said that for Ukraine, they amounted to to "time gained and lives saved. The less that reaches the occupiers, the less hits our warriors."
The collapse of the Crimean Bridge's arch was the worst damage to be inflicted onto the structure in several years.

The bridge had long been in Ukraine's sights because it represents Moscow's pretensions over sovereign Ukrainian land, and because of its logistical importance in supplying Russian troops in the occupied Ukrainian southern regions.
It was built and unveiled to great fanfare in 2018, four years after Russia illegally annexed Ukraine's Crimea.

Thursday's strike was carried out with Neptune cruise missiles, Ukraine said. Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge. Train services on the bridge were suspended but resumed in the afternoon.
Car traffic, however, will be prohibited for the foreseeable future as a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was dragged below into the sea when missiles hit the arch on Tuesday.
President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

The seven-stage operation first required the destruction of air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets which protected the bridge. Missiles and drones then dealt the structure the final blow.
Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack earlier this week
In response to Tuesday's hit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
But the operation to repair it could take a long time, and it will likely have to be carried out under frequent Ukrainian fire.
Russia has regularly targeted Ukrainian civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.
This week alone, as the Crimean Bridge was being hit, Moscow targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5dj: Watch: Moment Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m (£144.8m)
Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (£144.8m).
The sale of Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.

The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.
Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.
The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.
Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.
Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.
It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it in 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.
The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.
The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy: Pete Hegseth met Venezuela's interim president at the presidential palace

The United States and Venezuela have re-established military ties less than a year after US forces seized the then-leader of the South American country, Nicolás Maduro, in a raid on the capital, Caracas.
The interim government led by Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro's former vice-president, signed a military co-operation agreement with US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.
Few details about the deal have been released so far but Hegseth said that Venezuela had "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner" in less than 12 months.
Interim President Rodríguez said the deal would help confront "common threats".
Military co-operation between the two countries was terminated in 2005 by Hugo Chávez, Venezuela's left-wing president at the time.
Chávez alleged that US military personnel sent to Venezuela to train their counterparts had made disparaging remarks about his government.
He also accused the US military office located in Fuerte Tiuna, Venezuela's largest military complex, of being "an organ of the CIA... conspiring against the government".
Under Nicolás Maduro, who succeeded Chávez after the latter's death from cancer, relations between the two countries deteriorated further.
They reached rock bottom late last year when the US doubled its reward for information leading to Maduro's capture to $50m (£38m) and eventually seized him on 3 January in a military raid.
Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now in custody in New York on charges of drug-trafficking and conspiracy to commit torture , which they deny.
Hegseth addressed the change in the two countries' relationship since Maduro was seized in his speech at the US embassy in Caracas on Wednesday.
"It's a great honour to be here as the first United States Secretary of War this century to set foot in Venezuela. The weight of this moment does not escape me," he said.

"Just one year ago, my presence here, our presence here would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable," he added before recalling a public appearance by then-President Maduro which had angered the Trump administration.

"Exactly one year ago today, the indicted narco-terrorist fugitive Nicolás Maduro, the man who spent more than a decade handing Venezuela's borders and territory to terrorists from all over the world, stood on a stage, not too far from here, and yelled mockingly: 'Come and get me!'. Well, we answered that call."
Hegseth added that the result of the US military raid on 3 January had been as Maduro predicted, quoting the deposed leader's words: "No war, yes peace."

He described the deal signed by him and Venezuela's defence minister on Wednesday as a "new chapter for the United States, for Venezuela, for the Venezuelan military and for the Western Hemisphere through the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition".
Rodríguez described it as "extraordinarily relevant for our bilateral relations".

"In a matter of months, secretary, we have turned very difficult moments for our people into a space for co-operation and mutual benefit for both of our countries," she said addressing Hegseth during a meeting at the presidential palace.

While no details of the deal have been published, in her speech Rodríguez mentioned the training of Venezuela's armed forces and improving its "operational equipment" and access to new technology "to confront shared threats".

In his speech at the US embassy, Hegseth was more direct about who he considers to be those threats. Addressing "the narco-terrorists who abuse this [Venezuela] as a safe haven", he warned that "we will hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckdd: Susan Smith's ex-husband makes emotional appeal against granting parole
A South Carolina woman who admitted to drowning her two sons 32 years ago has been denied parole for a second time.
Susan Smith, 55, was convicted of killing her boys by strapping them into their car seats and rolling her vehicle into a lake in 1994.
"I got to my lowest when I let that car go into that lake," Smith said during a hearing on Thursday with the state board that decides whether to release those in prison on parole.

The seven-member board later unanimously turned down her request to be freed. The father of the two boys has vowed to continue to oppose her release, and several people spoke against her in the hearing.
Smith, whose lawyers had argued she suffered a mental breakdown during the crime, can apply to the South Carolina Board of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services for parole every two years.
She told the board that she had changed and matured since killing three-year-old Michael and one-year-old Alex, and that "I am not the same person I was 32 years ago".
She also said she was "very, very sorry" and that she would go back and change the circumstances if she could.
"They were innocent children," Smith said. "They did not deserve to die."
Her children's father, David Smith, attended the hearing so he could advocate for their sons, he said.
The 32 years, he said, do not take away what Smith "deliberately" did.
"I know in my heart granting her parole would be a huge injustice to Michael and Alex," said David Smith, who had pinned a photo of both his sons to his lapel.
Prosecutors argued during the trial that Smith killed the boys after a man with whom she was having an affair told her that her sons were the reason that the pair did not have a future together.
At Thursday's hearing, Smith said: "This did not happen because of a man. That's just not true."

When the boys first disappeared, Smith said she was carjacked late at night and a man drove away with her car. While she pleaded publicly for their safe return, her sons were at the bottom of a nearby lake.
Defence lawyers said she had wanted to die with her children but left the car at the last minute.
Smith was convicted of murder. Under South Carolina law at the time, she was allowed to request parole every two years after serving 30 years in prison.
In the US, some people convicted of crimes are eligible for parole, which means they can be released from incarceration.
She would have needed two-thirds of the board members present to vote in her favour to be freed.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9q: The US is playing catch-up with China's dominance in critical minerals mining and processing across Africa (file photo)
A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies from China and Australia.
The site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn), including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defence technology.
Frontier Minerals says its proposal aims to keep more of the economic benefits in Kenya through "processing and refining of minerals in-country".
The deal comes as Washington seeks greater access to Africa's minerals, aiming to strengthen US supply chains and compete with China.

Frontier Minerals brings together three US companies - Bunker Hill Mining Corp, American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies Corporation. The consortium combines expertise in mineral resource development, critical materials supply chains and advanced refining technologies.

A central part of its proposal is to develop mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya. Brad Barnett from Frontier Minerals said the company wanted the country to capture more value from its mineral resources.
Mrima Hill is located in Kwale County, near Kenya's Indian Ocean coastline. The site covers about 390 acres of forest.
The prospect of mining in the area has raised concerns among local residents, who fear the project could damage the forest and threaten their ancestral heritage.
There are also questions over whether communities living near the site will benefit from the investment.

Barnett was keen to reassure Kenyans that they would benefit: "We intend to create lasting opportunities for Kenyan workers, businesses and the wider economy through capacity-building and targeted investment, while prioritising environmental management and performance."
The consortium must still obtain a prospecting licence and meet the necessary regulatory requirements before the project can proceed.
The tender decision has drawn objections from competing bidders.
Reuters news agency reports that two rival companies intend to challenge the selection, with Australia's RareX alleging that Frontier Minerals missed an earlier submission deadline.
Kenya's government has maintained that the process was open and transparent.
The project comes as US strives to secure alternative sources of critical minerals and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the processing of several key minerals.

Washington has been pursuing partnerships with mineral-rich African countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, as it seeks to strengthen supply chains for industries ranging from electric vehicles to defence technology.
Kenya's mining ministry says the sector is an important part of its plans to diversify the economy beyond traditional sources of revenue such as tourism, agriculture and financial services.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c920: Bududa has suffered repeated deadly landslides over the years
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.
Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.
At least 33 of the 53 people who died in the 2019 landslide were children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.
William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family.
"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."
Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.
Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18m Ugandan shillings ($4,300; £3,300) to help them move to safer areas.
But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.

Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8m shillings, plus 10m shillings towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.
The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.
The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.

The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.
"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.
The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.
They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.
Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters.

"Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.
The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.
In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.

The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people.

"Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change – and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm70: Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty of all eight counts against him in a Florida court on Wednesday
A Florida pastor has been found guilty of a number of charges relating to the assassination of the Haitian President Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon, a dual US-Haitian national, was convicted of all eight charges against him, including conspiracy to kill or kidnap a person. He faces a potential sentence of life in prison.

The 67-year-old was accused of being involved in a plot to replace Moïse as Haiti's president with himself in 2021, allegedly so he could award lucrative contracts to a Florida-based security outfit once in place.
The murder of Moïse has left Haiti without a leader for five years. That political vacuum has intensified gang violence in the impoverished Caribbean nation.
A presidential election is scheduled for next year and Moïse's wife, Martine, who was injured in the attack that killed her husband, announced this week that she intended to stand.

Sanon was found guilty on Wednesday following an eight-week trial in federal court in Miami, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner. His lawyer said he maintains his innocence and that he intends to appeal against the verdict, it reports.

Prosecutors said Sanon had "political aspirations" in Haiti and, in April 2021, met several other co-conspirators to devise a plan to oust Moïse in an armed raid on the presidential palace in the capital, Port-au-Prince.

Among them were the heads of the companies Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security - collectively referred to as CTU - who would finance the coup in exchange for government contracts for infrastructure projects, and to provide security forces and equipment.

A few months later, the other conspirators realised that Sanon had "neither the constitutional qualifications nor the popular support" to become Haiti's president and so shifted to another candidate, the US Department of Justice said.
At the same time, the plot had developed from one to forcibly remove Moïse from office to assassinating him, investigators said.
Dozens of people have been implicated in the conspiracy, which prosecutors said involved co-ordinating funding for and delivering weapons and mercenaries to Haiti to carry out the attack.

On 6 July that year, a group of Colombian mercenaries entered the presidential palace and killed Moïse. His wife, who was also injured in the attack, said at the time that the assailants had "riddled" her husband with bullets.
Jovenel Moïse was gunned down by mercenaries in Haiti's presidential palace in 2021
The successful assassination plot raised questions in Haiti about the relative ease with which the mercenaries were able to gain access to the president.

The country - the poorest in the Americas - has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but Moïse's assassination ushered in a period of worsening instability that emboldened gangs and prompted the deployment of a multinational force.
However, this has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway and more than 5,700 people have been killed or injured in the year to 11 September, the UN said last month.

Sanon and several other co-conspirators were arrested by Haitian authorities, while three mercenaries were killed in a gun battle with police. Eighteen people were transferred to Florida in September to stand trial over the plot.

Four men, including the heads of the CTU, were convicted of their role earlier this year. Sanon had been scheduled to be tried with them, but his case was delayed due to health reasons, according to CBS.
Sanon was born in Haiti but moved to the US as a teenager. He told the court he had worked in churches in Haitian immigrant communities in several parts of the US including Florida, US media report.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8r: Residents fled the area near Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps following the Israeli evacuation order
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.
Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.

In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".

Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.
An image, meanwhile, showed six armoured vehicles, including tanks and bulldozers, around Salah al-Din road.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Multiple verified videos of the aftermath of the incursion on Thursday showed destruction, earth banks, and heavy vehicle tracks more than 1.2km beyond the Yellow Line.
That is believed to be the furthest Israeli troops have advanced into central Gaza since they occupied the so-called Netzarim Corridor before the ceasefire.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9q: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.

The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor , giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.
The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.
Musk was speaking virtually , external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat.
"I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.

For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.
In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.
Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.

In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings , as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.
Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According to BBC analysis , Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Musk said on Wednesday that he believes Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, is "going to be quite moderate".
Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than three decades of the party's control of the state.
The Tesla boss added : "I don't think she's a far-left governor. And based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."
Democrats won Congress in a blue wave. Now comes the hard part.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq20: The alleged foreign agent was discovered with two Russian passports
A Russian man has been arrested in California's Silicon Valley for allegedly attempting to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm that supports the Ukrainian military.

Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a covert operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco. The BBC understands that the company targeted was Palantir Technologies.
D'iu is also charged with stalking employees and possessing falsified identity documents.
The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia.

"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian.
"We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations."
Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.

He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine".
On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.
He then went to a coffee shop located near the company's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there.

His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".
The suspect allegedly took photos of employees screens at a cafe near the office
A source in the industry confirmed that Palantir was targeted, and added that the operation did not penetrate the company's private systems.
They added that the company has been "targeted extensively" by Russia over its involvement in Ukraine, and that the attacks are becoming "increasingly aggressive".
The source, who did not want to be named, said that this was the first time a Russian operative was found while on US soil attempting to spy on the company.
"I think the surprising thing is that they decided to take the risk of sending someone to the US," they said, in an attempt to get into the system "physically".
Palantir has not issued a statement in reaction to the charges.
D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences.

On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.
During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".

A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up two Russian passports, and a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say.

He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.

The revelation that Robert Pattinson is the new Bond caps off an incredible run for the British actor, but will he satisfy fans of the long-running franchise?
Pattinson will be the first actor to take on the role of the super-suave MI6 agent since Daniel Craig’s departure.
How did British actor Robert Pattinson go from Twilight to James Bond?
But one glaring detail remains: this Bond is still a man, still British, still white, and presumably still upper-class.
Is this who Bond is destined to be? How much can James Bond change before he stops being James Bond?
Rumours have circulated for years regarding a potentially diverse Bond, whether that’s someone who isn’t white, or a woman.

Based on the character by Ian Fleming, Bond has previously been played (in chronological order) by Sean Connery, David Niven, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, and Daniel Craig.
Broadly speaking, the onscreen Bond represents the refined man’s male power fantasy.

He moves through the world through his signature suaveness, stealth, and social aptness. He’s an urbane master manipulator who drives an Aston Martin. He can conquer just about anything, and do so with grace and sophistication.

He’s also a perpetual Lothario, and his propensity for womanising is one of his foremost tools for gathering intelligence and infiltrating places he ought not be. Only some entries see him fall prey to a femme fatale, rather than dominating the dynamic.
Perhaps the most interesting thing about Bond is that, until the advent of the films, he was intentionally lacking in characterisation.

Fleming served in the British Royal Navy’s Naval Intelligence department during the second world war, so Bond is supposedly inspired by many of his own experiences - a composite of the spies he met throughout his espionage career. In 1962, Fleming told The New Yorker he "wanted Bond to be an extremely dull, uninteresting man to whom things happened".

He notably gave the character some more context in his penultimate novel You Only Live Twice (1964) - released after the first film - such as having a Scottish father and Swiss mother, while also adapting some of Sean Connery’s inadvertent Scottish characteristics into the novel.

Aside from this, Fleming’s physical descriptions of Bond, such as being possessed of “dark and cruel good looks”, and resembling American musician Hoagy Carmichael, still leave a fair bit of wiggle room in terms of casting choices.
Previous iconic performances from Scottish (Connery) and Irish (Brosnan) actors show us it is not Britishness by birth, but rather the performance of Britishness, that defines James Bond.

There’s no reason the Bond of the new era needs to be white. There are plenty of debonair British men of just about every race, colour and creed who could fit the bill of being “dark and cruelly good-looking”.

Nine senators wrote to the Pentagon this week saying further maturation of New Zealand's space programme and additional investment would advance US national security objectives.

This would help "ensure allied and partner space superiority by providing opportunities for additional satellite tracking, space surveillance, missile coverage, and communications redundancies," they wrote on Tuesday (US time).
New Zealand already played a "crucial role" in US Space Command operations running a space-watching hub in Auckland and supporting partner nation training around the world, they said.

Congressional records show Senator Eric Schmitt introduced an amendment in July for the Pentagon to produce a strategy within six months to enhance US-NZ defence cooperation, including for more shared space and military industrial efforts.
He singled out addressing shared security challenges in the Pacific and the Antarctic.
His amendment was submitted but does not appear to have gone further though it had called for a strategy by the end of 2026.

The senators wrote to the Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink on November 17 asking him to consider extra steps to improve space efforts with New Zealand, "a key Five Eyes partner, where doing so advances US national security interests and strengthens collective capability".

Meink in September publicly acknowledged for the first time the US has deployed weapons in space . The US Department of Defence describes China as its "pacing" or number one threat militarily and in space.
Major General John Howard, now a consultant, said New Zealand should embrace the senators' call.
The fact the likes of Russia might not like it should not put people off, he added.

"If this was a simple aviation issue or a simple commercial offering in one of our primary sectors, we wouldn't be thinking twice about it. Russia has previously warned it considers other countries or commercial satellites that help Ukraine in the war to be legitimate targets.

"Someone sitting in Moscow wishing to rattle a sabre would be thinking carefully about what that means," said Howard on Thursday, "and today's a great day to ask that question, because we're seeing three leaders meeting in the edges of APEC , and they'll be having all sorts of discussions on relationships."
Any move to get closer to the US when many countries regard the Trump Administration as a less reliable security partner was a question for MPs, he said.
"The reality here is we live in a world that has risk no matter which way we turn.

"The decisions of who we support, who we align with, and who we share technology with, those are decisions for the Cabinet table, the National Security Board, and the boards and chief executives of those companies."
New Zealand should be happy it was being acknowledged this way by Congress, he said.
However, Wellington peace activist Valerie Morse said it was one-sided.
"This letter from the US senators makes no mention of New Zealand's interests, only US security interests.

"We need to understand that New Zealand is being groomed as a US military outpost for its space operations, that's what this letter is about, it's clearly about advancing US security interests," said Morse on Thursday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4g: Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?

Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."
The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.
Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is selling shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.
The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.
So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?
At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".

The company is selling roughly $81bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta from StoneX trading.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."
What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.
It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.

Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?

"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgl: Photonic chips use light instead of electrons to process data
"Photonic chips are on the verge of a breakthrough," says Ton van Mol of the Dutch research institute TNO.
If van Mol is right – and TNO, the European Union and the Dutch government are backing the idea with millions of euros - then the technology could be a gamechanger.
The chips which run today's society, from your phone and TV, to the vast data centres meeting our insatiable desire for AI, are mostly electrical.

They process data by shunting electrons around tiny circuits – a single microchip produced today can contain billions of transistors, and sizes are measured in nanometres (one nanometre is a billionth of a metre).
Because they use light instead of electricity, photonic chips are faster, use less energy and generate less heat than traditional computer chips.
Van Mol hopes for an acceleration in photonics similar to the one seen in electrical chips since the 1970s.
"With optical chips, you are now where electronic chips were maybe 40 [or] 50 years ago."
American, Taiwanese and Chinese firms dominate the computer chip industry, but Europe sees the emergence of photonic chips as a fresh opportunity to lead, on what could be, a key future technology.

Which is why the European Union has committed €400m ($450m; £330m) to a project called PIX Europe , external , with the stated goal of making the continent "a global leader in emerging technology for Photonic Integrated Chips".
"Europe said 'we need to have our own manufacturing in-house'," says van Mol, who is leading a key part of the programme.

"We cannot depend like in the past that everything is manufactured in the US or China - that's not wise, so the [European] Chips Act was called into life, and one of the parts of the act is to build pilot lines to really bring the technology, which is now in labs, to the next stage - manufacturing."
Electronic and photonic chips are produced on wafers made up of hundreds of individual chips. Factories with machines that can handle bigger wafers can churn out chips more efficiently.
"[Photonic chip] manufacturing worldwide is [currently] done on wafers which are four inches (10cm) in size, and the next step is to scale-up production to a six-inch wafer," says van Mol.
His team are already building a 10,000 sq m factory to produce six-inch indium phosphide wafers on the High Tech Campus in the Dutch city of Eindhoven.
It's due to fully open in 2030 and will be a major step forward, not just for photonics in Europe, but around the world, according to van Mol.
"That's the development TNO is going to do, in a pilot line which is really serious.
"In 2030, we hope that we have a stable, reproducible, high-yield process, and then the intention is that the pilot line [opens] to industrial parties who can make commercial production out of it."
Netherland's based ASML is a crucial supplier of chip-making equipment
Europe does have one crucial player in the current computer chip industry - ASML.
The Netherlands-based tech giant is the only company in the world able to build the machines needed to make the most sophisticated semiconductors.
Which is why ASML products will sit at the heart of the pilot line in Eindhoven - it's no coincidence that van Mol's project is based around the corner from ASML's headquarters.
"The way you produce these [photonic] chips is very similar to the way you produce electrical or electronic chip," says van Mol.
"You use the same type of equipment, you also need a high-end clean room, you also use wafers, so the production method is very similar to the traditional semiconductor technology."

Fifteen survivors escaped from the 56-metre (184ft) luxury yacht and managed to get to a life raft that had been launched by a crew member.
The marine investigation found that the Bayesian "had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down".
In addition, "the extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk", Loder added.
In the early hours of 19 August 2024 the Bayesian was anchored outside of Porticello port, on the north coast of Sicily.
With thunderstorms rapidly coming in, wind speeds went from 8 knots to about 70 knots (80mph) within minutes. The weather forecast had only predicted gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph).
The MAIB report stated that with no sails set Bayesian was vulnerable to being knocked over in severe winds.

It also found that any knockdown - where the boat was suddenly tipped sideways - would be "irrecoverable once the yacht passed the angle of vanishing stability", assessed in the study as being 73 degrees. Once the vessel passed this angle it could not right itself.
The wreckage of the Bayesian off the coast of Porticello, Sicily

In addition, the centreboard, which provides stability when a ship is under sail, was raised. The report said the centreboard was not needed when the Bayesian was using its motors and was rarely lowered at anchor. The way the boat was loaded, and the angle of the wind, also contributed to the accident.
Inspectors said a "downburst of hurricane-force winds" was the most likely cause of the ship keeling over.
They happen when cold, dense air plunges rapidly, sending out violent winds across the surface.
The MAIB said that none of risks were covered in the UK training syllabus, nor in published guidance available to crew.
Once the vessel was on its side, it rapidly filled with water and sank.
As it heeled over, five people were injured, either by falling or by items falling on them and a deckhand was thrown into the sea, the report said.

As water started entering the yacht, two of the guests "used the furniture drawers as an improvised ladder to exit into the central alleyway", then climbed along the internal walls to get into the saloon.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy: The Scottish government is facing questions about its plan to issue its first ever bonds.
The move would allow ministers to borrow money from investors who in return receive regular interest payments.
The aim is to raise about £1.5bn by the end of the parliamentary term, with the funds to be used on long-term projects such as building hospitals or maintaining roads.
Named "kilts", a nod to UK government "gilts", the scheme has provoked much debate.
This week, MSPs on Holyrood's finance committee heard about the potential risks and rewards.
A bond is a financial tool used by a government to borrow money. They are sold with a promise for the buyer, or investor, to be paid back at the end of an agreed term.
The government will also make regular payments to the investor.
In the UK, a government bond is called a gilt. They are typically bought by financial institutions such as pension funds, insurance companies and commercial banks.
As a play on this term, the Scottish bonds have been nicknamed "kilts".
The Scottish government has said it expects the bonds to be issued within this financial year, subject to market conditions.

Former First Minister Humza Yousaf commissioned initial work in 2023 after advisers in the Scottish government's investor panel recommended making bonds available to the market as a means of raising Scotland's profile and attracting investment.
In November last year, the government announced that it had received an identical credit rating to the UK's score.
This was based on "prudent fiscal management" and the country's economic stability - though ministers were warned this could change if Scotland moved towards independence.
With market volatility due to conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, some have questioned whether now is a good time to launch bonds.
But at Holyrood, David McMillan, professor in finance and accounting at the University of Stirling, told MSPs: "You can't wait for a perfect time because there's going to be no perfect time."
The government wants to raise £1.5bn through bonds by 2031, although that would only be a fraction of its near £70bn budget.
About four-fifths of the Scottish government's budget is used on resource spending, which goes towards day-to-day costs such as funding the NHS, benefits payments and paying salaries.
A smaller portion is made up of capital spending, typically used on long-term physical assets such as buildings and bridges, or maintaining roads or paths.
The Scottish government is unable to borrow for resource spending other than to correct forecasting errors.
However, for capital spending, it can borrow as much as £450m a year at 2023-24 levels up to a total cap of £3bn - to be uprated with inflation.
Adjusted for inflation, the government could borrow about £491m in the current financial year, with a total limit of about £3.3bn.
Economists have noted that Scottish bonds would be a more costly way of borrowing than existing routes provided by the UK government through the National Loans Fund.
It has been estimated , external that interest rates on "kilts" would be 0.3 percentage points above gilts, plus an additional £2m per bond in administrative costs.

The Scottish government has not released costings, citing market sensitivities, but has insisted , external issuing bonds would represent value for money relative to the costs of borrowing through the UK scheme.
Ministers argue that issuing bonds would be a good opportunity to market the country to investors, and would be helpful if Scotland became independent.

Dr Ben Cormier, a senior lecturer at the University of Strathclyde's department of government and public policy, told Holyrood's finance committee that while the Scottish bonds could cost marginally more than the UK scheme, they would "bring flexibility to public finances and debt management".
