https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy4: Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to jump by £443 a year from January as the inflation rate rose to its highest level in a year.
A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, ahead of the official announcement next week.
Some households will get a £100 payment to help with the rising cost of living, a policy which was announced in the Budget.
Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices, official figures show.
Inflation has been driven higher in recent months as the US-Israel war with Iran has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.
In response to prices surging, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month, in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%.
Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.
Higher interest rates lift the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings.
Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs.
VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand £100 to 20 million homes in January.

But with annual household energy bills forecast to reach £2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East".
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: "Affordability is my number one priority, and I will continue driving towards cheap, clean power."
Sophie, who manages a cafe in Brighton, told the BBC she watches her smart meter at home "like a hawk".
"I'm very conscious of the cost of energy, and it is having an impact on how we function in the home as a family," she said.
"I try to cook using the oven a lot less than I used to. We haven't got the heating on yet in our household. We're just like 'wear more layers'. We've got electric blankets on the sofa."
Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you
Shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, said four successive rises in the inflation rate was down to the UK's "soaring energy costs" and Labour's decision to "hike taxes and employment costs".
Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said fuel prices were "once again a major contributor" to the increase in the inflation rate in October.
Rising energy prices can lead to more expensive food and staples for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs.
Earlier this month, the Bank of England said there had been "limited evidence" of this, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower profit margins.
But Fitzner said on Wednesday: "Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively."
Petrol prices rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October, the ONS said, with the average price last month hitting 174.7p per litre - the highest since August 2022.
Diesel prices, meanwhile, reached the highest price since records began 30 years ago, averaging 199.5p per litre in October.
But the ONS said price inflation in restaurants and cafes had slowed last month, and that prices had fallen on average for hotels.
And food price inflation rose by 0.9%, the slowest pace in five years.
Core inflation, which strips out energy and food costs, and services inflation were little changed on last month. The figure is closely watched by the Bank of England when setting interest rates.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c674: Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.
Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.
The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.
Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.
The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

The company's $1.5tn estimated valuation is on a "diluted" basis, a broader reflection of the firm's value that takes things like employee stock options into account. On a basic share count Anthropic is worth about $1.1tn, more valuable than Walmart and Samsung but less than Tesla and Meta.
But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.
But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.

Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".

In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.
Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.
The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei co-founded firm five years ago

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.
While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.

Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.
Anthropic was started by seven former OpenAI employees, led by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei.
Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the risks posed by AI, amounting in his view to a possible threat to human existence.
The company has called for a slowdown in the development of AI, and a greater focus on safeguards while forging ahead with plans to grow quickly and boost its financing through the public markets.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckq6: Nobody will be celebrating the fact that prices in the UK are rising at the fastest pace for a year.
Add to that an expectation of higher household energy bills and sharpening price increases and things look grim for everyone.
But there are some signs of hope that may take the edge off the rising cost of living. Here's how.
That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%.

Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year - that's an increase of £443 from current levels.
Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights.
How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit.
The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support.
The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation , external , as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills.
While the rate of inflation in general was 3.6% in the year to October, food prices only went up by 0.9%.
It is partly the result of intense competition between the supermarkets. Like many retailers, they are facing higher costs but are not passing that onto their customers in full.
There may be some scars from the recent cost-of-living spike here. Shoppers suffered a period during the big rise in inflation in 2022-23 when food prices rocketed.
Those higher prices are embedded. While food prices overall aren't coming down now, they aren't rising anywhere near as fast as back then.
The detail here is very interesting. Take chocolate: world cocoa prices are down since 2024, and now chocolate prices are falling - down 2.9%, according to the latest data.
But the ONS has also pointed to cat food as one, albeit small, driver of the faster rate of rising prices.

Should high energy and fuel costs - which are driving the rising rate of inflation - persist, there are questions over whether the cost of producing and transporting food also goes up, and the chances of that higher cost being passed on to consumers are greater.

Economists have been closely studying whether there are any signs of those so-called second-round effects - where an initial price shock spreads to wages, services and broader consumer prices. So far, there are relatively few.

If prices rise then it takes a bigger chunk of people's income and so has a deeper impact on those whose finances are already stretched, so the latest data on food prices is good news for many people.
Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again

One set of economists who will consider whether there is evidence of second-round effects are the nine people who set interest rates, which heavily influences the cost of borrowing money - such as mortgages - as well as the returns people get on savings.
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets again in December and, after that, in February.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2k: Nvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn.

In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, covering the three month period just before the recent scandal surfaced, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it was "business as usual". She told investors: "We've got this."
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.
But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones said: "The board does not intend to reinstate him."
Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.
The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn.
The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.

"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".

"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."
The interim chief executive also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.
The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.
Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him
Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.
He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.

"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new chief executive will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c687: Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.
The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending.
Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says.

"If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says.

Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run.
That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?
That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back".
Huang himself has said he is open to a return, just days after resigning .
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y: Watch: Jeff Bezos on involvement in casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond
Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond.

Speaking at an event in California, the Amazon chairman said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in many blockbuster films like Batman and the Twilight series - "because he's already so famous".
The role of 007 has typically gone to an actor who is not as well known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond".

This will be the first 007 film in the official series not under the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since the first movie in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM, which co-owns the franchise, in 2022.
'Good Bond vibes' - Hollywood locals react to Robert Pattinson cast as new 007
"There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."
The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

Robert Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday
Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.
But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckq6: The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.

It said in its tests of six glasses available on the Dutch market, the devices advised a user on how to date a child, misread medicine instructions, and claimed to have called an ambulance when they had not.
While the AP is advising people not to buy the smart glasses, it stopped short of calling for them to be banned from sale.
The authority is not revealing which glasses it tested, saying only that prices ranged from under €100 (£84) to over €500 and originated from different continents.

The research follows growing concerns about privacy risks associated with smart glasses, in particular the misuse of the tech to film women without consent , or to record in places where filming is usually prohibited such as healthcare settings.
Meta, a leading seller of the glasses, recently released a version without a camera with some commentators suggesting this was a response to the privacy backlash.
It is unknown if the investigation included Meta's glasses. The AP told the BBC it would not name the products it tested.
The BBC has approached Meta, TCL and HTC - all major manufacturers of smart glasses - for comment.
Previously, these firms have been keen to highlight positive uses of smart glasses.
Meta has highlighted the assistance they can provide to people with visual impairments. Its smart glasses use AI to describe things in the wearer's environment or to read text.
The AP recognises the glasses can be valuable for people who need help to understand their surroundings.
But for these users, it argues it is particularly important that AI is reliable.
AP said in its testing of the unnamed brands, it found the advice given could be wrong.

During a simulated emergency in which CPR resuscitation advice was requested, the AP found one pair of glasses claimed several times an ambulance was on the way - but emergency services had not been contacted.
It said the AI also made child protection errors, with potentially serious consequences.
One pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who indicated a romantic interest in a minor.
The glasses also made errors when reading instructions inside medicine packages, as well as with interpreting severe weather warnings.
And the AP was concerned smart glasses could be used to secretly film people, highlighting the ease with which lights, which warn that a device is recording, could be obscured.
It said with some glasses these lights could be covered with tape and they would still work, despite some manufacturers claiming they would not function.
Meanwhile, in some glasses, the AP found serious security flaws which meant someone nearby could connect without permission, view recordings, or even operate the camera remotely.
It warned data recorded by the glasses was often exported outside the EU.
In February, reports revealed outsourced workers were able to view sensitive content recorded on Meta smart glasses
Meta said at the time such workers might sometimes review content, including video and images, in order to help improve its AI .
It said it took the protection of people's data very seriously, and was constantly refining its efforts and tools in that area, and would filter it first to blur faces in images.
The AP investigation was not primarily focused on data protection - instead it was concerned with algorithms and AI.

In the UK Paul Arnold, chief executive of privacy watchdog the Information Commission, who has a severe visual impairment has previously stressed the complexity of the argument , external around smart glasses.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6z7: After years of anticipation and delays, as well as controversy around worker rights, Grand Theft Auto 6 has completed its phased worldwide release and is available to gamers everywhere, including the UK.
There has been near universal praise from critics, with review aggregator Metacritic calculating its average score at 99 out of 100 based on 150 reviews. , external
Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has held the top spot since 1998 - but Metacritic confirmed to the BBC that this has now officially been overtaken.
GTA 6 is set to become one of the world's most popular entertainment products ever, with fans booking time off work, and schools warning students not to bunk off.
Some schools have reminded parents and pupils to prioritise study over the game, which has an 18 rating , external for "strong graphic violence, strong sexual themes and use of illegal drugs".
One school in Essex incentivised pupils to attend with prize s such as vouchers, Christmas dinners and a pass to skip the lunch queue.
The UK rating means it can only be legally sold to an adult. It does not stop an adult letting their child play the game - instead it is meant to inform their decision.
It's the game that shocked and thrilled the world: Grand Theft Auto. As a new installment is released in 2026, go deep into the history of the game with rapper Bugzy Malone.
The game, set in the fictional US state of Leonida, follows two protagonists, Lucia and Jason, through the seedy underbelly of America after an "easy score goes wrong".
It was released at midnight in all the countries it is available in, which meant New Zealanders were the first to access it.
"The graphics are great. Even from the set-up and credits, it's feeling pretty good," Aleana Fernando, who lives in Auckland, New Zealand, told BBC Newsbeat soon after she started playing.
Once the game was released at midnight UK time, gamers were equally enthralled by the game's graphics and attention to detail.
Charlie Wood from London said he had "already laughed at the dialogue before even stepping into the gameplay".
About 30 minutes into playing in Leonida, he said it was "most definitely worth the wait".
Meanwhile in Germany, Timur told the BBC he was impressed by how lifelike the game was.
"It really feels like a life simulation with the amount of in-game encounters," he said.
The Guardian's Keza MacDonald , external was impressed by the relationship between the main characters.
"GTA has never been particularly kind to women... there is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI's world, but now we have Lucia to react to it," she said.
"This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story".
From the memes to the music - from the controversies to the culture - you have your say on GTA 6 with Newsbeat's Jordan Kenny and De-Graft Mensah.

After GTA 5 became one of the most successful entertainment products of all time - with estimates of net profits soaring as high up as $10bn (£7.6bn) - anticipation could not be higher for the sixth instalment.
Makers Rockstar North, headquartered in Edinburgh, delayed the release twice, saying it needed extra months to finish the game with the level of polish fans had come to "expect and deserve".
The company was also set back by hacks and leaks of its unfinished version.
On Monday, 21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, pleaded guilty to the Rockstar Games hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.
He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished and hugely anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8r: Review scores for GTA 6 are a fairytale ending after years of development
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.
Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?
Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100 , external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.
Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.
Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."
But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN , external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".
Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.
"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote , external , but he added "there are also nits to pick".
For The New York Times , external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.
Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.
But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.
Critics say the relationship between Jason and Lucia is central to the game

The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian , external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".
And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.
"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".
Writing for Forbes , external , Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".
The Washington Post , external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg , external 's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.
"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.
"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."
Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m).
Gaming journalist Jordan Middler is one of the lucky few in the UK who got early access from Rockstar and tells BBC Newsbeat it is the "game of a generation".
He'd played for about 100 hours by the time he hit the credits and says he still has so much to do.
Middler did spot one negative though - he found the game can "slow down" because of how much is going on.
He also says it is "long overdue" that there is a female lead in Lucia.
"The way previous GTA games have dealt with women has been a boys' club approach," he says.
"Introducing Lucia and not making her some kind of token character, she just fits in completely... and she will quickly become a fan favourite without question."
The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6z0: Outages and IT failings are commonplace - but not on this scale.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage , an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours , and issues for the National Security Agency (NSA). That's not to mention outages affecting the biggest US banks , as well as a major flaw found in a popular programming language .
These are all separate incidents - but the fact they have all come so close to each other has got people wondering if they might be linked.
There is no evidence to suggest this - but they do tell us a lot about how the modern tech world works, and where the vulnerabilities lie.
As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or installation going wrong somewhere in a system.
A network upgrade at Microsoft caused servers to become overloaded and shut down.
It was also upgrades to a creaky old network which grounded thousands of planes in the US over the weekend.
Problems with the NSA's internal communication system and, separately, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay were also blamed on things going wrong during system updates.
Disruption to payments in US banks has been put down to a "software bug" from JP Morgan Chase. The bank says it is not a cyber-security incident.
But some recent problems are in fact related to cyber-security vulnerabilities.
AI was used to discover flaws in Java, the third-most popular programming language in the world.
And researcher Scott Helme also discovered malicious code in Optimizely, a platform which is used by some of the world's largest companies.
Hackers were able to steal about $7,000 (£5,300) in cryptocurrency before they were discovered and kicked out.
Let's address the cyber incidents first - and the role of new AI models.
"I would be very surprised if all of these cyber-attacks and the attackers behind them were not using AI to accelerate themselves," Helme told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Since the summer, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have decided it's too risky to give the general public access to the most advanced models before allowing certain companies and institutions to use them.
In these cases, security professionals can use the same tech to find flaws themselves and alert others before criminals get to them.
This happened in the recent Java incident , as well as the PHP one - where there was a scramble to patch the flaws before they could be exploited.
These are not new - the world stood still in recent years as CrowdStrike and then Amazon Web Services ground many devices and systems to a halt.
Part of this may be down to technical debt - a term used when operators go for quick fixes to software instead of solving an underlying problem.
A build-up of surface-level fixes can eventually end up with more serious problems down the line.
With AI causing many companies to re-evaluate their cyber-security, they may be issuing more updates to patch flaws they have found.
Outages are often also a reminder of the physical tech our online world relies on - such as cables, servers and data centres.
In the US air traffic control incident, for example, the problem came as engineers were replacing outdated copper wires with fibre.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is adamant the recent incidents are not connected or coming from one attacker.
"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."
In cases such as PHP and Java, the "good guys" found the flaws, with the help of AI, before the bad guys - allowing them to get together some fixes before the bugs could be widely exploited.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm87: A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.
US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.
The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.
Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.
Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.
It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.
Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.
The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.
The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".
The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.
The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.

For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.
The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.
In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.
Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.
In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency.
Cyber security researchers and journalists reported that he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch.

"TylerB and his group were highly sophisticated and organised but the violence he and others experienced was a sign of the troubling direction of these online communities of young hackers" says cyber security researcher Allison Nixon from Unit221B.
Buchanan then reportedly fled to Canada to escape further threats before returning home.
In April 2023, officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI.
Investigators recovered a device containing the names and addresses of hacking victims, along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.
He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples.
After being extradited to the United States, he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.

In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to the notorious cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cke8: A tech start-up used AI to uncover a critical software bug in Java that had existed for more than a decade (generic photo)
A cyber-security firm has used artificial intelligence (AI) to uncover a critical flaw in the hugely popular computer programming language Java.
Tech start-up Calif - which recently identified a cyber-security flaw in another language, PHP - found the bug in Java's memory functions.
Java is a popular programming language used by nearly all of the world's top companies such as Apple and Amazon, as well as many banks, hospitals and governments.
It is meant to make the IT world more secure by managing your memory online, said computer scientist Professor Toby Walsh, which is why "this is such an unlikely and serious flaw".
The discovery comes after a string of serious technology issues, including a massive Microsoft outage .
On Tuesday, the US National Security Agency said its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to a "scheduled routine maintenance".
The NSA did not specify whether its outage was linked to the identified Java bug.
Apple also reported multiple services suffered full outages due to an internal update, while a network failure grounded all flights in the US.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the incidents were related .
With the help of AI, Calif discovered a serious security vulnerability it has called Java4Shell, which allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands to Java's memory system.
In this case, the adversary was OpenAI's recently-released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public.
Oracle, the owner of Java, released a "critical patch update" on Tuesday, which it said contained security vulnerability fixes - including for this flaw.
At this stage it is unclear if any platforms or companies have been affected by the latest incident.
But the Java flaw remains a huge concern for cyber-security experts, who say overloading a system's memory is one of the most common ways for hackers to exploit or crash a system.
What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
US National Security Agency's classified internal network reportedly goes offline
Nearly every critical sector, including banking, national security systems, aviation and telecommunications, relies on Java.
First released in 1995, the programming language and computing system is now the "beating heart of the modern economy", Calif said in its investigation.
One of its main functions is to manage and protect memory for you, Walsh, a leading researcher in AI, told the BBC.
Any time you transfer information on the internet, receive a file from a user or need to log into an IT system with a password, the platform you are using is likely relying on a Java program.
The serious flaw could comprise "critical financial systems, customers and organisation's data," cyber-security expert Dr Pedram Hayati said.
In Australia alone, almost every bank uses Java for managing critical transaction data, Hayati added.
The latest incidents have exposed how nearly every critical sector - including national security systems, aviation and telecommunications - relies on legacy infrastructure online.
Earlier this week, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services.
The Java discovery follows a critical cyber-security flaw identified in the PHP programming language, also identified by Calif.
PHP is the code that websites like Wikipedia use to collect information and present it in a way you can read on the web.
Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the PHP flaw affected some 30 million websites, leaving them vulnerable to malicious attacks.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy8: Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.
The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.

California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.

Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.

California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".

In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.

The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".
A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."
Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.
Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.
The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United head coach will be at Liverpool on 22 November
"We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."
Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.
The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.
He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.
The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.
Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.
So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?
"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.
Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator
Fitness obsessed & 'control freak' - what can Man Utd expect from Pochettino?
Matheus Cunha's injury-time goal against Roma on 3 November sealed one of only three Manchester United victories in 15 games this season

It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.
Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.

United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.
One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.
"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.

"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.
"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."
Diogo Dalot is consoled by Manchester United team-mate Joshua Zirkzee after being substituted during the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa
That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.

The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.

Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.
New Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino (right) worked with his full squad for the first time on Thursday

Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.
Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cricket/arti: Pat Cummins spoke to the media on 12 November, calling Usman Khawaja's claims over the sandpaper scandal "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense"
Australia captain Pat Cummins, much like his fellow bowlers, is in the eye of the sandpapergate storm at the moment.

The reason is simple to me. The very notion that Cameron Bancroft - the most inexperienced batsman in the Australia team at the time – would use sandpaper on the ball against South Africa without the bowlers knowing has never made sense.
It has never seemed remotely plausible to me, as a former bowler, that the bowlers didn't know what was happening in Cape Town in 2018. It just doesn't seem possible.
Let's be clear - as long as there has been cricket, there has been ball-tampering. There is no point hiding from the fact.
Back in the day it was about shining the ball, maybe using something like a sweet to get a sheen on one side.
Reverse swing was a ball-tampering game-changer. There was a requirement for a wearing process, roughing up and drying the ball.

But, to get one thing straight, whether a ball is being tampered with or not, it belongs to the bowlers. It is the bowling attack's weapon. As much as a bowler would not fiddle with a batsman's bat – sanding an edge or changing the grip - a batsman would not work on the ball without the knowledge of a bowler.
Some might wonder why revelations relating to the sandpaper controversy have not come to light before.
In response to that, I would say it would have been very difficult for a player in the Australia team to go public at the time. They would have been worried about their own futures, their careers.
Only when a player has retired, or believe their time as an international cricketer has come to an end, do they feel more comfortable to speak up.
I have also seen suggestions that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner have had their guilt diminished by what has emerged in recent days, that they took bullets for their team-mates.
Smith was captain and should have been in control of his team. Warner cooked up the sandpaper idea. Bancroft executed it. If they did take bullets, they were bullets they deserved.
Now, the spotlight has fallen on Pat Cummins, whose agent has repeated his client's version of events in the last 24 hours.
The junior bowler at the time, Cummins has ascended to the captaincy, often joked to be the second-most important job in Australia, behind only the prime minister.

Cummins is not a typical Australian captain. He is not abrasive, or in your face. When he says he has worked hard to correct the image of his team, he is credible. Then again, he missed a trick to really prove Australia are no longer a win-at-all-costs outfit with the Jonny Bairstow stumping in the 2023 Ashes Test at Lord's.
After everything he said in public, and the way he has been backed by Cricket Australia (CA), there seems to be no obvious suggestion Cummins has considered resigning, or that he will be sacked.
He is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on 9 December.
Looking ahead to that match, it is difficult to see how the build-up will be anything other than a circus, dominated by questions about sandpaper, who knew what and who said what to whom.
The litmus test for Cummins will be the public reaction. Remember, that Test is being played in Bancroft's home city, in the state of the newspaper where his 4,000-word testimony was first published.
If Cummins is still in his position by then, the response of the Perth crowd to the captain will be very interesting.

Even if Cummins does get through that, the Australian media will not let up. This is a huge story, one of the biggest in the history of Australia sport. The press will bang away until they feel they have got the truth.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/golf/article: LIV Golf - backed by more than $5bn (£3.8bn) from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund - paid millions to players and executives in the weeks before filing for bankruptcy, while leaving a trail of unpaid bills from UK suppliers.
BBC Sport has seen invoices from five small businesses totalling hundreds of thousands of pounds, all of which were overdue before LIV made its final payments to players.
Global Infusion Group, , external a Buckinghamshire company that provided catering at July's LIV Golf UK event, is still owed £321,671, due on 7 August.
Suffolk-based BD365 Clean , external provided 108 cleaning staff and is owed £75,225, most of which was due on 20 July and 13 August.
"It just feels completely immoral," said Bonnie May, chief executive of Global Infusion Group.
"It really matters to a business of our scale. The impact has been huge, both personally and professionally."
Only $2m (£1.5m) has been earmarked so far by the Saudi owners to pay unsecured creditors, leaving many smaller companies unsure if they will receive anything at all.
Yet court filings reveal LIV made 59 payments to golfers on 31 July, amounting to $16.6m (£12.6m) and matching prize money for the same LIV Golf UK event.

A further $34.2m (£25.9m) went to players between 17 August and 3 September following tournaments in New York and Indianapolis, including $6.4m (£4.9m) to 2026 champion Jon Rahm just five days before the bankruptcy filing.
Four senior LIV executives also received retention bonuses totalling nearly $3m (£2.3m) in August.
"It's sickening," said Krissi Foskett, owner of BD365 Clean, who described the unpaid bills as "almost an extinction-level event" for her team.
"How can they sleep at night, knowing they are potentially putting companies out of business?"

Meanwhile, public records list more than £3,000 owed to Goodysphere, , external a family-run Yorkshire firm that provides a sensory bus designed to help autistic children who may find busy events overwhelming.
However, in August, LIV chief executive Scott O'Neil said he hoped they would be able to pay their suppliers.
"What I would say to them is we're doing everything we can to make sure we can do right by them and the work they committed."
Players received a total of $16.6m (£12.6m) five days after the LIV Golf UK event
The controversial breakaway league had been owned and bankrolled by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) since its launch season in 2022.
But in April, the fund announced it would end its backing after the 2026 season, putting LIV's future in doubt.
"Our understanding was that the funding would take LIV through 2026," said Global Infusion Group's May, whose company had about 60 staff catering for players and broadcasters.
"We weren't aware the funding had already stopped and there wasn't enough to actually fulfil their obligations."
PIF's multi-billion-dollar investment helped it to lure some of golf's biggest names and disrupt the PGA Tour's dominance of the sport.
"It's Saudi money, that's safe as houses, we thought," said Foskett.
"Their head honchos came along and enjoyed hospitality. We were there cleaning up at one o'clock in the morning then back in at five in the morning, only to be treated like this."
PIF remains the majority owner of Newcastle United, while Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 Fifa World Cup.

"I'm sure the country won't want to be saddled with the characterisation that it doesn't pay its bills," said professor Simon Chadwick, who is an expert in the business and politics of sport across Africa, Europe and Asia.
"I do find it surprising that they would simply walk away. I think they would want to engage in some kind of remedial action, particularly in terms of managing their image and reputation."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Manchester City have won the Premier League on eight occasions
Premier League clubs have voted to cover legal expenses for the organisation's five board directors if any of Manchester City 's sponsors sue them.
The clubs met in London on Thursday for the first time since City were found guilty of a catalogue of charges relating to the breaching of financial rules by an independent commission in September.
City have appealed and maintain their innocence, with a sanction yet to be decided.
The club's sponsors Etihad and Etisalat have both said they are considering legal action against the Premier League.

At present, under the league's articles of association, a director is only financially covered should they win a legal case brought against them by a third party. But the league's rules will now be updated to extend legal indemnity for CEO Richard Masters, chair Alison Brittan and three other non-executive directors .
City and Nottingham Forest were the only two clubs that voted against the proposal to provide extra legal protection, with the other 18 clubs voting in favour.

Due to collective responsibility, it means that all clubs are now liable to cover legal costs that could run into hundreds of millions of pounds, raising the intriguing possibility of City being financially impacted by the legal action of its own sponsors.

It is understood City's CFO Ingo Bank asked Premier League chair Brittan during Thursday's meeting if the proposal was a direct result of threats of legal action from Etihad and Etisalat, but she said she could not comment.
While Forest have declined to comment, their objection to the proposal is said have to been on procedural grounds, rather than due to any support for City.

The club did not believe that sufficient information had been provided, or adequate time afforded, for clubs to properly consider the implications of the proposed amendment, particularly given the potentially significant financial responsibilities involved. It felt that such a decision warranted more scrutiny and informed consideration before clubs were asked to vote.
An independent commission appointed by the Premier League found City guilty of artificially inflating the club's revenues by over £830m over a nine-year period in September.
The commission determined that the club arranged "sham" contracts with sponsors, which disguised funding from club owners the Abu Dhabi United Group.
Premier League CEO Masters said City "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade".
In October, City sponsor Etihad Airways said it was considering legal action against the Premier League .

In a statement, the United Arab Emirates-based airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".
Etisalat signalled its intention to follow suit earlier this month and described the Premier League's verdict as "entirely false and defamatory".

Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.
In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.

That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.

In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.

His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.

Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.
Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.

Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.
Kane scored his first England goal 79 seconds into his debut in 2015
Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.

Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'big six' clubs.
Only second-placed Brighton , a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton , have muscled their way in.
The six biggest clubs - Manchester United , Liverpool , Manchester City , Arsenal , Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.
BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.
Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.
In England, Liverpool , Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.
Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea , Manchester City and Tottenham .
This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.
We will use Everton , the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.
This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.
In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was £120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to £442m.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool , told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.
"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."
Only 10% of Everton 's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.
It means Everton , and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.
For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.
But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.
It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.
This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.
But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.
When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.
This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or £713m, for the historically most successful clubs.
At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned £37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool £35.5m and Chelsea £33.3m. Newcastle received only £13.6m.
The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.

That's the message from Māori artist and rugby league supporter Charles Williams, who told RNZ the celebrations surrounding the Rugby League World Cup are about something much bigger than what happens on the field.
Despite the Kiwis suffering a big loss to the Kangaroos in the final, across Tāmaki Makaurau and beyond, supporters took to the streets waving flags, singing and celebrating their whakapapa.

At the centre of many of those celebrations was Williams (Ngāti Kahungunu ki te Wairoa, Te Whakatohea, Tūhoe, Ngāpuhi), who organised a series of parades to bring people together in support of the Kiwis.
The idea was inspired by the passion of Tongan supporters during the 2017 Rugby League World Cup.

"2017, the Tongan fans really took fandom to another level. So they went all out and they were basically riding solo. During that 2017 campaign, we saw them all over the streets of South Auckland, where I live.
"Post World Cup, I went to Tonga, did an art project over there, got to meet them and got to see even more the fan base there and how crazy they are.
"Come 2026, I really wanted us to kind of just get off the couch, really get out of the house. Let's be inspired by our whānau from Tonga, Samoa."
Williams approached New Zealand Rugby League with the idea and rallied friends to help bring the parades to life.
It began with around 50 people gathering at Māngere Bridge during the first week of the tournament. By the second week, the crowds had grown to hundreds, and the flags kept coming.

"I've noticed in this World Cup, there's been more of an emphasis on, yeah, hey, I'm from Tonga, Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, so on and so forth. And even guys who are not a part of the Rugby League World Cup are jumping in.

"Guys from Niue, all of a sudden you got yellow flags all over the streets. They want to be proud of themselves and everyone wants to be proud of themselves. They want to stand up and go, 'Hey, here I am, here we are and we're from here.'
"And that's awesome, you know, and I love it. And I want people to really be proud of where they're from."
But the parades also prompted a bigger reflection for Williams about how Māori come together as a people, and how those gatherings are perceived by others.
Māori flags, including the Tino Rangatiratanga flag and He Whakaputanga flag, are often seen at hīkoi and protests, where communities gather to advocate for their rights, identity and rangatiratanga.
Williams said some people mocked the parades online, questioning whether supporters were protesting or taking part in a hīkoi.
And while he understands why people might make that association, he said the celebrations offered a different opportunity to come together under the same flag.
"One thing I've been thinking about for a little bit is how do we celebrate as a people? So we're kind of like known as the 'fighting people'.

"A lot of the comments mocking us were, oh, are you guys protesting? You know what I mean? And it's like, cool. "You know, I understand why you say that, because literally, we are always protesting. But it's been the first time, not the first time ever, but it's like the first time I've seen thousands of people with a Tino Rangatiratanga flag, happy, celebrating, and we're not actually fighting for anything.
"We're not trying to like get anything. It's just like, bro, we're just happy."
"We're under this flag. We're under this banner. And to celebrate, it's just been like, finally, we're just like, we're just happy."

The All Blacks say they're happy with the way hip and knee drop tackles are being officiated after Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus was suspended for criticising match officials.

World Rugby has banned the 54-year-old for six games for his post-match comments after South Africa's 21-19 defeat to France last weekend, in which he questioned whether officials were manipulating the game.
Erasmus, who has a long track record of publicly criticising match officials , believes they failed to notice, or ignored, up to 17 illegal tackles in Paris.

Hip tackles (a defender putting his weight on the lower limbs of an attacker in the act of bringing him down), and knee tackles (a defender starting the act of making a tackle while on one or both of his knees) was made illegal by World Rugby on 1 November.
All Blacks wing Leroy Carter required ankle surgery after being caught in a hip tackle during his team's Bledisloe Cup victory at Eden Park in October.
"The TMO (television match official) doesn't come in once. I'm not saying he's wrong. I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem," Erasmus said after the test.
"If he saw it and he decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing? Is that not interfering with the outcome of a game?"
Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus will miss this weekend's test against Ireland.

South Africa Rugby has confirmed Erasmus will request a full misconduct hearing in order to "contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives".

The All Blacks also believe some illegal tackles went unpunished in last Sunday's 35-28 loss to Wales in Cardiff, with stand-in captain Beauden Barrett heard on multiple occasions asking referee Pierre Brousset about the hosts making hip drop tackles.
However, All Blacks hooker Asafo Aumua, speaking ahead of his side's clash with England at Twickenham on Sunday, said officials were largely getting it right.
"I think there were a few missed ones on the weekend, but that wasn't going to really change the result in the game," Aumua said.
"I feel like they're [match officials] doing enough, we've just got to be a bit more accurate in our tackles."
Aumua said he didn't think players intentionally made hip or knee drop tackles, but added they could be hard to avoid in a sport as dynamic as rugby.
"On the weekend, I felt like I'd nearly done maybe two [hip drop tackles], but not on purpose," Aumua said.
"I just got beaten on the outside and grabbed them and ended up swinging around, so I just let go."
Aumua said the best way to minimise illegal tackles was to focus on technique.
"Just getting in front [of the attacker] and trying to get them going back instead of swinging around."
As it stands, Erasmus is set to miss the Springboks clash with Ireland this Sunday and their Nations Championship playoff match the following weekend.
The ban is set to expire during next year's Rugby Championship, meaning Erasmus will be back in the hot seat in time for their World Cup title defence in Australia, which starts next October.

Voicing Luke Skywalker in the Welsh-language version of Star Wars was a "dream job" according to actor Osian Morgan.
The Cardiff-born actor said he loved the film series as a child and playing one of the lead roles was "very exciting".
Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd - based on the original 1977 film Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope - was given its first showing at a red-carpet event in Cardiff on Thursday.
The dubbed Welsh version, featuring actors Matthew Rhys and Rhys Ifans, will be broadcast publicly for the first time by S4C on Christmas Day.
Almost half a century since A New Hope was first released, the sci-fi universe created by George Lucas remains one of the biggest film franchises of all time.
It has been translated into over 50 languages, with Welsh becoming its most recent.
"It feels very exciting, it's thrilling," said Morgan, who has previously starred in Welsh language soap opera Pobol y Cwm and in BBC drama Waterloo Road.
His family attended the first screening of Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd, and Morgan admitted his youngest brother had never seen any of the films before.
"Shout out to him because the first time he gets to see it in Welsh is great," he said.
The red-carpet event in Cardiff included a rousing version of the theme tune

Mark Lewis Jones, who voices the dark lord Darth Vader, said on the red carpet it was "nice to record the voice but not have the make-up" and joked that "the Rhosllanerchrugog accent lends itself to the dark side".
Llyr Ifans, who plays C-3PO, said he hoped the film was successful and that more Welsh-language versions would follow.
"I'm quite confident it will go down well and there will be a lot of happy Welsh-speaking parents on Christmas Day."
Ifans said he been a fan of the Star Wars films since childhood, and getting invited to play the character was "surreal".
"When I first got the email through I thought 'wow, this is a bit weird doing Star Wars in Welsh' but playing C-3PO, one of the iconic parts, you can't say no, can you really?"
C-3PO is said to be fluent in six million forms of communication and Ifans said it was now one more.
Mark Lewis Jones, who voices Darth Vader, joked his accent 'lent itself to the dark side'
Prominent actors have lent their voices to the film's most famous characters, including Matthew Rhys (Han Solo), Rhys Ifans (Obi-Wan Kenobi) and Aimee-Ffion Edwards (Princess Leia).
Other voice actors in the Welsh version include Nia Roberts, Ioan Hefin, Richard Harrington, Owain Arthur, Rhodri Meilir, Richard Elfyn and Steffan Donnelly. The film is directed by Ellyn Stern.
The Welsh language version was announced at the National Eisteddfod in Pembrokeshire in August
The Welsh-language version was announced at the National Eisteddfod in Pembrokeshire in August, with Lucasfilm co-president Lynwen Brennan saying the franchise was keen to expand its horizons.
"As someone who was born and raised in Wales, seeing the audience reaction to iconic Star Wars moments retold in the Welsh language was a moment of great pride," she said.
S4C chief executive Geraint Evans added that working with "one of the most iconic and influential film franchises of all time is a tremendous honour".
"It is a unique opportunity to introduce the Welsh language to new audiences around the world, while showcasing Wales and its exceptional creative talent on a global stage," he said.

But when pressed by the reporter if he wanted to change the law to take action, he replied: "I wouldn't leap to that. I would first say to the social media companies show some responsibility here, think of the victims - that's the main thing.
Google told BBC News it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".
It added: "We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6eq: The band have become known for their energetic live performances and interwoven four-part harmonies
Westside Cowboy have been announced as BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026.
Jimmy Bradbury, Reuben Haycocks, Aoife Anson O'Connell and Paddy Murphy formed the band in Manchester in 2023 and have since rocketed from the pub circuit to some of the UK's biggest festivals.

The award is presented to an up-and-coming artist or band who has, with the support of BBC Introducing, made a significant impact and has previously been won by Olivia Dean, Myles Smith and Tom Grennan.
Murphy, from Longridge in Lancashire, said the win put them in "good company", with Bradbury, from Shropshire, adding that it was "very flattering".

BBC Introducing supports new musical talent across the UK , providing a platform to propel new artists on to the local and national stage through 30 Introducing shows, three national radio shows and six shows across BBC Radio 1, Radio 1Xtra, Radio 2, 6Music, Radio 3 and Asian Network.
About 72,000 tracks from emerging UK artists supported by BBC Introducing make it on to the airwaves each year.

Westside Cowboy uploaded their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You) to the Introducing platform in November 2024 and had their first play on radio within hours.
Murphy and Bradbury were surprised with the award during a radio interview
The four-piece played in various other bands before coming together to form Westside Cowboy.
Haycocks, O'Connell, and Murphy had met at Manchester's Royal Northern College of Music in 2021 and later got to know Bradbury after meeting him in the nearby Johnny Roadhouse music shop.

Murphy and Bradbury played in surf-rock trio Katz, while Murphy and Haycocks both worked together in noise-pop trio, DieKaiDie, but it was when Bradbury, who was working in the music shop repairing guitars, asked the others if they wanted to start a new band that Westside Cowboy's journey began.

By the time their second single, Shells, was released in April 2025, they had been been selected to play the BBC Introducing stage at Glastonbury Festival, and the song was put on the BBC 6Music playlist.

Their meteoric rise saw seen them appear on BBC music show Later... with Jools Holland in June and their debut album It Goes On was released on Island Records in August, peaking at number five in the UK charts.
Westside Cowboy reminisced about the early days on BBC Radio Manchester
Thanking the Introducing network and listeners for their support, Murphy said it was "really cool to be recognised for the music you make".
"We say this a lot, so apologies if we sound like a broken record, [but] it's funny with this band because... we started it with so little pretence or plan," he said.
"So whenever people give us something cool like [this award], it's all a bit surreal because it still feels like a weekend project that we now just get to do way more regularly.
Westside Cowboy formed in 2023, having played together in other bands
William Wolstenholme, presenter and producer of BBC Introducing in Lancashire & Cumbria, gave the band their first play and said he remembers messaging them to upload the track.
"Over the past two years, Westside Cowboy have become surely the most exciting band in Manchester, and therefore the country," he said.
"They've fast-tracked from the sweaty pubs of the city's student music scene to many of the most famous venues in the country.
"It's a rise whose speed can scarcely be believed, and one that has shocked much of the music industry."
He said the band's obvious camaraderie was one of their main selling points.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqj3: Page spoke of the inappropriate comments during Tuesday's episode of the reality show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here!
