https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6x2: Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members
Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.
The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.
Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations .

But in a statement published on Wednesday , external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.
He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.

But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".
Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.
The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.
In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.
The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario , external and television network Univision news, published in January.
In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.
The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.

Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.

The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.
Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.
In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said , external : "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."

On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".

It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g: Freja, who "didn't expect to be chosen" as the winner, beat more than 1,000 entries from across the UK
A teenage Hunger Games fan has met the cast of the new film after her artwork won a competition, meaning it will be displayed at every cinema screening across the UK.

Freja Brown, 13, won the British Board of Film Classification's (BBFC) create the card competition, which ran ahead of the release of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping - the sixth film in the franchise.
Freja, from Cardiff, beat more than 1,000 entries from across the UK and said she was "so grateful" to be chosen.
Her design will be the official BBFC black card, which displays the age rating and classification details of the film before every cinema showing.
Freja's winning design will be shown as the official BBFC black card before every UK cinema screening
The Year nine student, whose favourite subject is art, only started oil painting three years ago.
Her mum Marie recalled the moment Freja found out about the competition while scrolling on social media.
"She just squealed and said, 'there's this competition where you can create a piece of art' and she loves making art. So, she was like, 'I'm gonna do it'."
"She's read all the books and watched all the movies, so being able to combine her love for the Hunger Games with her own art sounded really fun."
Freja and her mum attended a fan screening event for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on The Reaping in London
Joseph Zada, Mckenna Grace, and Whitney Peak, who play Haymitch, Maysilee, and Lenore Dove in the new film, announced Freja's winning design in a specially recorded video.
Freja said: "I couldn't believe it. I knew that there were lots of other people who had sent in their artwork, so I didn't expect to be chosen and I am so grateful I was."
As part of her prize Freja was also invited to attend a screening of the film in London, where she met some of the stars.
Showing the work to Elle Fanning, who plays Effie Trinket, the actress said: "Oh my God, I thought it was a photo."
Actor Ralph Fiennes said: "It looks wonderful, it's really amazing, I love it."
Freja only started oil painting three years ago, but her mum says she has always been a creative person

Speaking of her inspiration, Freja said: "I was inspired by this specific part in the trailer because it shows the Hunger Games arena to be a beautiful place and not the killing machine that it actually is."
Marie, who is a photographer, said her daughter has always been a creative person and "makes stuff all the time", filling their home with her creations.
Marie said her daughter spent more than a month on the piece and worked until the day of the deadline after she "locked in for a whole weekend" to get it done.
"It's not just a random piece of art somewhere, it's something that her and her friends get to see, which is fantastic."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9vg: Reviews of the latest Hunger Games film have seen it dismissed as a "surreally awful prequel" and "a tortuous, costly mess" by some critics - but called "surprisingly strong" and "one of the best films in the series" by others.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson.

In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film , external "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase".
But the Wrap praised its , external "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best."
Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the first Hunger Games film, and 40 years after the previous prequel, 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.
"This prequel lands at some mid-point between Ballad and Hunger Games, which puts it on an immediately odd footing," Empire said in a three-star review , external .
"It can't escape the sense of feeling supplementary. It's an enjoyable-enough diversion, but essentially a footnote with aspirations."

Screen Daily called it , external an "underwhelming prequel", which "suffers from a lack of compelling characters" and "feels oddly incidental - a drab afterthought rather than a crucial new chapter".
The film's all-star cast includes Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace and Maya Hawke alongside Joseph Zada as the 16-year-old Abernathy.
IndieWire , external said Zada's performance is "charming enough", but "his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films".
The movie feels "a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series' lore" and is "a dreary slog", IndieWire's critic wrote.

The New York Times , external also used the word "slog", adding: "One really misses the guiding presence of Jennifer Lawrence, who had the raw pathos to both ground and expand a world in a way many younger stars often can't.
"In Sunrise, we're instead left with fleeting moments in which Plemons or Ralph Fiennes (playing the evil President Snow) briefly elevate the film. They seem to be trapped in this dystopia too."
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will be released this weekend
However, the Hollywood Reporter , external was more enthusiastic about both the film and Zada's performance, calling it a "star-making turn".
Its critic concluded: "Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes, to the spirit of the first movies."
And Time Out's four-star review , external said the film is "as strong as any" of the other movies, and "certainly a major step up from 2023's drab prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crx2: Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.
Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.
The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.
Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.
NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.
In the end, more than £30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.
But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.
Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.
This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.
They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers. Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.

The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.
When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.
In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.
Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.
Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.
But it was not until September in England – and later in Scotland and Wales – that £500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.
More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.

Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett. That didn't happen.
The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".

Although the closure and restriction of borders was noted as "immensely complex", the inquiry said that border control measures could serve as an important tool "to reassure the public and increase confidence."
By April 2020, 93% of countries had put measures in place, such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions, to control their international borders.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8wy: More than 200 doctors have had their details sent in error to the Times newspaper
The doctors' regulator the General Medical Council (GMC) has apologised after it mistakenly sent information about more than 220 doctors to a national newspaper.
The information included summaries of complaints alleging antisemitism or Islamophobia against the doctors.
For some of the medics involved, it was only when the GMC alerted them to the data breach that they discovered a complaint had been made about them.
The GMC says it is "very sorry" for the incident and has reported itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

The GMC - an independent body that regulates doctors, physician associates and anaesthesia associates to protect patient safety - sent the information about 223 doctors to a journalist at the Times newspaper.
While no names were revealed, GMC identification numbers were included, which would easily allow doctors to be found on the regulator's register.
Some doctors have also raised concerns that their ethnicity was included in the data breach.
All the medics involved have been the subject of a complaint involving either antisemitism or Islamophobia, dating from the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 to September 2026.
The GMC says it has a legal and statutory responsibility to investigate such claims.
Meanwhile, the Times is understood to have promised not to make any of the details public, but has said it will not delete the information.
A spokesman for the doctor's trade union, the British Medical Association (BMA), condemned the release of personal information.

"The BMA is aware that a number of doctors have received communication from the GMC to say that it erroneously sent personal identifiable data about them to the Times newspaper when responding to a media request," it said.
"The GMC must take action to ensure such a breach never occurs again."
The BMA said it would look at ways to support members affected and urged them to make contact via their website.
A doctors' campaign group, The Doctors' Association UK (DAUK), called for an independent investigation into the error.
"If a doctor sent identifiable patient information to a newspaper, they could expect to be referred to the GMC," said Dr Matt Kneale, DAUK co-chairman.

"The GMC should hold itself to the same standard of confidentiality it expects from doctors. It owes every affected doctor a clear account of what it sent, how that happened and what it is doing to get the information deleted."

The doctors' regulator says around a fifth (20%) of the complaints made have already resulted in some sanction related to antisemitism, including two doctors who have been struck off the medical register.
Just over a quarter of complaints over Islamophobia - 26% - have led to disciplinary action.
But other complaints were closed, having failed to reach the threshold for investigation.
The GMC said it had contacted the doctors affected to explain what had happened, to apologise and provide information and support.
A spokesperson added: "We recognise the concern this will cause to both those impacted personally and other registrants and we are very sorry this happened.
"Our priority continues to be supporting those affected and taking steps to reduce the impact of this incident."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pw: Adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone are allowed but must be rooted in evidence, the regulator said
Five adverts by online healthcare provider Voy have been banned by the watchdog for making misleading claims linked to low testosterone in men.
The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said the adverts promoted Voy's at-home testosterone blood tests in three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads.
It said they were misleading as they linked common symptoms such as irritability and fatigue to low testosterone.
Voy said it had withdrawn the adverts while the investigation was under way and would not run them again.
The NHS says that while testosterone levels in men fall as they age, this is "unlikely" to cause any problems in itself.

It adds , external that while a testosterone deficiency in later life can sometimes be responsible for symptoms such as depression, loss of sex drive, erectile dysfunction, and other physical and emotional symptoms, they are often not linked.
Voy is a company that sells products such as testosterone, menopause and weight loss treatments.
Some of its testosterone test kit adverts drew a backlash online earlier this year when they appeared on the London Underground.
Some described them as "ragebait" for using phrases such as "It's not him, it's his hormones" and "Men get hormonal too".
At the time Voy said it was trying to destigmatise conversations about men's health.
Some of the adverts sparked discussion online after appearing at Tube stations
The ASA's ruling, however, took issue with how some of the adverts "exaggerated the connection between several common symptoms, which can have many possible causes, and low testosterone".
The ASA gave examples such as low sex drive, low energy, loss of motivation and changes in mood.

"While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn't have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation," the watchdog said.
It added that one of the Facebook adverts also included the claim that "low testosterone sneaks up on 1 in 4 men over 30".
The ASA said this was misleading and not supported by the evidence provided by Voy.

Dr Earim Chaudry, chief medical officer for Voy, said: "Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance."

Wednesday's ruling followed two others in August by the watchdog, which found misleading claims in adverts for testosterone testing services from online providers BioID Health and Numan Digital Healthcare.
The rulings form part of a wider ASA investigation into adverts aimed at men concerned about their health.
This has identified a "recurring theme of advertisers playing on insecurities around libido, erectile problems, testosterone and ageing", the regulator said.
The watchdog said adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone were allowed, but businesses needed to make sure the claims they made were accurate and supported by evidence.

Dr Richard Quinton, who is an expert in testosterone deficiency, said: "It's very easy to get a low testosterone level in any healthy man, simply by doing a blood test in the afternoon, after a meal, when unwell from any cause, or after an all-night sit up."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm0e: From Spring 2027, under 16s will no longer be able to access several social media applications
More than 300,000 young people in Britain will work with researchers to help understand how the UK's forthcoming social media ban for under-16s could affect mental health.
The studies will examine the habits of the children and teenagers, including whether they spend less time on their phones and what they are replacing scrolling with.
Ten different projects have been commissioned, taking place across England, Wales and Scotland, to help reflect a diverse range of teenagers.
The social media ban, beginning in spring 2027, will follow a similar model to that already introduced in Australia to stop children accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
Apps such as Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Snapchat and YouTube will be banned under new rules
The work, funded by health charity The Wellcome Trust, will help inform future online safety policies in the UK and internationally, with some early results available before the ban happens.
Researchers will use wearable technology, smartphones, digital diaries and surveys to collect data to see how young people respond to the ban, both physically and mentally.
And they will check whether young people find ways to circumvent restrictions.
Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome, said it was a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media and its restrictions affected youth mental health.
"We really don't think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don't work.
"Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people's digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing."
Participants are being recruited to reflect a diverse range of young people, including different genders and sexual orientations.
People with existing mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression, will also be included, as well as young people who are neurodivergent.

Groups have been set up at Cardiff University, the University of Oxford, the University of Birmingham, King's College London, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Manchester, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and University College London.

There have also been reports of Australian teens finding ways to get round the ban - with the UK government promising to make sure tougher blocks are in place.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg: The government says it will continue a key NHS data contract in England with the controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029, rather than triggering an early release clause next year.
But ministers are inviting British firms to bid for the contract from 2029, with a procurement programme beginning next summer.

A Commons Committee had called on the government to part ways and appoint a company "more compatible with UK values". Protesters regularly target Palantir over Israel's use of its technology in the Gaza conflict and oppose its use in US immigration enforcement.
The £330m deal, which began in 2024 to help manage hospital waiting lists in England, was due to run until 2031.

The prime minister had faced pressure from some Labour MPs to cut ties with Palantir. They said they were extremely disappointed by the decision, calling the contract "an albatross" hanging around the NHS's neck.
There have also been concerns raised about how patient data will be used .
Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.
Health minister James Frith said the move was "not about the politics of executives of suppliers, nor is it about the territories or customers that one company or one supplier makes".
The government says UK companies will be encouraged to tender to avoid overdependence on one supplier.
The timeframe is not fast enough for some members of the government.
Dame Chi Onwurah, Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the government needed to "act urgently" to procure "credible domestic alternatives".
"The government should not wait two years, it must start reducing this dependency now," she said.
Former Labour shadow chancellor John McDonnell went further, and accused Palantir of "human rights abuses". He said his constituents in Hayes and Harlington "expect the contract to be ended".
Liberal Democrat health spokeswoman Helen Morgan criticised the company for what she called its "appalling human rights record, run by an ally of Donald Trump".

The British Medical Association, which represents doctors, said it was glad the government had shown it was listening to its concerns about Palantir, but was frustrated the process of changing to another company was further delayed.
Palantir UK said it was right to press forward with the programme which was exceeding targets.

"We are proud of our work to date to help deliver more operations, speed up discharge and reduce the time patients need to wait to find out if they have cancer," Palantir UK senior vice-president Tom Watson said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2: Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences"
The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she does not support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.
Baroness Cass told BBC Radio 4's Today programme while it is "desirable" to ban the practices, "the challenge is that we have not yet as far as I can see got a workable bill".

At a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, she also said it risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.
They added they would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right". The government has said the bill would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.
Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.
This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.
There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.
When the government introduced its draft legislation , external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it , external .

In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not."
She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.
But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".
Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.

The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities".
But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.
"Therapeutic interactions can be distressing and often are because you're discussing quite sensitive issues," she told the Today programme.
"So If a young person comes away feeling upset, distressed, angry, that might be the result of a quite appropriate therapeutic intervention but still could be judged as poor professional practice."
She told the committee that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.
"The problem is the chilling effect of professionals knowing that they may be open to complaint, and indeed prosecution," she told the Today programme.
Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.

She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.

Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but had not had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqjd: Nicola Packer was acquitted of "unlawfully administering to herself a poison or other noxious thing" with the "intent to procure a miscarriage"
Women arrested or convicted for having illegal abortions will have their criminal records wiped as new automatic pardons come into force in England and Wales , external .

Ending the Victorian-era law should avoid traumatic experiences such as that of Nicola Packer, who was recently cleared by a jury after taking medication at home during a Covid lockdown. She had ended a pregnancy without realising she was around 26 weeks pregnant, far beyond the legal 10 week limit.
Her friend Helle Tumbridge told the BBC's Today Programme she had been "treated appallingly" until justice was served.

Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalisation amendment last year, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who have been "unnecessarily harmed" by an "outdated" law.
Ms Packer, who was 41 at the time, took pills called mifepristone and misoprostol, which were prescribed over the phone due to Covid restrictions, to end a pregnancy in 2020.
Prosecutors alleged that she knew she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which she denied.
Jurors deliberated for more than six hours to reach their unanimous verdict, clearing her name.
Speaking with the BBC and Nicola's consent, her friend Ms Tumbridge said the whole incident was "incredibly traumatic".
"Nicky had what's known as a cryptic pregnancy - that's when you don't have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms.
"She thought she was just a few weeks pregnant and she sought an abortion and was prescribed that by the NHS. Unfortunately, she was a lot more far gone."
Nicola experienced a stillbirth and went to hospital. The staff there called the police.

"She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly. She was made to use the toilet with the door open in front of the police officers."
It took five years of investigations for a trial to eventually find her not guilty.
"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," says Tumbridge, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."
At the time, The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said Nicola's trial demonstrated "just how outdated and harmful" that law was.
It is now no longer a criminal offence for a pregnant woman to terminate her own pregnancy at any stage.
Minister for Victims and Tackling Violence Against Women and Girls, Alex Davies-Jones, said pardoning women for abortion offences related to their own pregnancy had been a priority.
"I'm pleased to be able to commence the change that Parliament voted for.

"For those affected, I know that clear and accessible information about what happens next is vital. Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team."

Heidi Stewart, from the abortion care provider BPAS, said: "While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice."

Abortion in England and Wales is legal with an authorised provider up to 24 weeks, with very limited circumstances allowing one after this time, such as when the mother's life is at risk or the child would be born with a severe disability.
It is also legal to take prescribed medication at home if a woman is less than 10 weeks pregnant.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y: The capsule dissolves in the stomach and releases a small sponge which collects cells from the lining of the oesophagus as it's removed
Some people with bad and persistent indigestion should be offered quick "sponge in the gullet" tests to check for oesophageal cancer, new draft guidelines for the NHS in England recommend.
The sponge tests can be carried out in GP surgeries in minutes, and are less invasive than hospital endoscopy checks that instead use a small camera to look inside the body.
The tests are already available in some places but could now be offered across England.
Heartburn or acid reflux can occur with a condition called Barrett's oesophagus that increases the risk of cancer in the long term.

It is thought between one and two adults in every 100 has Barrett's oesophagus, where cells have started to change. Most won't go on to develop cancer, but demand for NHS endoscopy is high, meaning some with the condition aren't checked as often as recommended.
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says the sponge tests, already offered in some places, could help give more patients peace of mind.

For the test, patients swallow a small dissolving capsule attached to a thread. Once in the stomach, it releases a tiny sponge. The sponge collect cells from the lining of the gullet as it is gently pulled back out of the patient's mouth by the doctor.

Prof Jonathan Benger, chief executive of NICE, says sponge tests offer a "quick and less invasive" way to detect concerning changes, helping to identify people who should go on to have further tests and treatment.

Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said: "The NHS is always looking for better ways to get to the bottom of people's symptoms, and thousands have already benefited from this incredibly efficient test through pilots we have been running, so it's fantastic it is now being considered for roll out across the country.

"Many people have acid reflux, and having an easier way to check for changes in the lining of the oesophagus can make a big difference for patients, reducing the need for more complicated endoscopy tests and helping the NHS free up resources to find cancers at an earlier stage."
However, no diagnostic test, including endoscopy, identifies every case and people who receive an all-clear sponge test result should still be monitored in the long term, NICE adds.
The sponge tests can help detect oesophageal cancer and Barrett's oesophagus in people with reflux disease.
The oesophagus leads to the stomach. Both are highlighed in red/orange
Reflux can cause heartburn, which is a burning sensation in the middle of your chest, as well as an unpleasant sour taste in your mouth, caused by stomach acid.
A lax or weakened sphincter at the bottom of the oesophagus or food pipe, where it meets the stomach, can be part of the issue, allowing digestive juices to seep up the wrong way.
Being overweight, smoking and drinking alcohol can increase a person's risk of reflux.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwr7: The Conservatives have promised to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework in a bid to limit the use of AI by schoolchildren in England if the party returns to power.
The party has also pledged to develop new guidelines so that laptops and tablets are not the "default in classrooms".

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott cited recent warnings from clinicians that excessive screen time could be damaging children's health, adding that "everything in schools must be safe for children and improve standards".
The government is currently developing new screen-time guidance for children and has previously said it would consult on the safety of AI in schools.

The vast majority of school exams in the UK are pen and paper based. Under the previous government led by Sir Keir Starmer, exam regulator Ofqual launched a consultation last year , external on the introduction of on-screen exams.
But it emphasised that pen and paper would "remain central" and that the most widely taken subjects would not be moving to digital assessments for the "foreseeable future".

In their announcement on Sunday, the Tories said they would "put a stop" to the introduction of screen-based exams, and require screen time for secondary pupils to be limited to no more than two hours a day.

The party said it would also minimise the amount of coursework in school assessments to avoid lowering educational standards "by allowing children to become overly reliant on the use of generative AI platforms".
Under the plans, primary schools would be required to keep screen use to a minimum and only use screens where necessary, such as in computing lessons.
Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under stricter rules for schools in England

The announcement comes after a group of more than 150 clinicians warned last month that the amount of time children in England spend on screens at school could be harming their "physical and developmental health" .

An open letter to Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Health Secretary Yvette Cooper from the clinicians said they were prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children "for a problem that is unintentionally being made worse in our schools".

Trott said: "I want to slash screen use in classrooms and set a new norm where screens are no longer the default. That means no screens in early years, minimal use in primary schools except where required by the curriculum."

Figures from the most recent government survey , external show that in 2024, most teachers (89%) used interactive whiteboards within lessons. But the survey also found that most teachers - 79% in primary and 69% in secondary - said pupils were using individual devices in fewer than a quater of lessons, or not at all.
The Tories said their plans draw on the work of the Health Professionals for Safer Screens campaign group, which has warned about the effects of excessive screen time on children.

Its founder Dr Rebecca Foljambe said: "We have become excessively preoccupied with why children are on screens. Although content is important, this distracts from the fact that daily screen time can profoundly affect a child's health, whatever they are watching or doing."
As part of its proposal, the Tories said £900m that "the government currently spends on EdTech" would be repurposed to create a £250m fund for new textbooks.

A Department for Education spokesperson said schools decided how much to spend on educational technology, which alongside screens also included things such as management information systems, from within their own budgets.
"It is up to schools to decide how they use their funding in the best interests of pupils," they said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg: Key services across the UK, including the NHS, GPs and schools, have been affected by a global Microsoft outage.
Pharmacies and businesses have also been hit after email and messaging services went down.
NHS England said patients should still attend appointments unless told otherwise, while several large police forces are urging the public to call if they want to report a crime.
Microsoft said services were now gradually being restored globally after a problem caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers, but users could still experience disruption.
The government said it was working closely with the firm to assess any impact on its services, while local authorities warned that some council services were being affected.
The full extent of the impact of the outage - which is affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot - and the time it will take to restore the systems remains unclear hours after users first reported issues.
The chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents the healthcare system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said the outage was affecting some services including emails.
NHS trusts in England were enacting measures to minimise disruption to critical services, a spokesperson said.
Patients have been told to continue to use 999 in an emergency and otherwise contact 111 by phone or online, or their local pharmacy.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains. Practices in Hampshire and Shropshire have told patients to phone them or come into the surgery if they have an urgent need.
Microsoft scrambles to solve global outage affecting Outlook and Teams but says fixes not going 'as expected'

A National Pharmacy Association spokesperson said the outage was affecting pharmacies' ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients, so "waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions".
The overall impact on health services remains unclear. Much of the NHS calendar is linked to diaries using the Microsoft system, but workflow practices differ between hospitals and trusts.
There are anecdotal reports of c-sections being cancelled and hospitals only accepting urgent referrals - though the impact on elective treatments has yet to be confirmed.
The GMB union's national secretary Rachel Harrison said the outage was having a "serious impact" on ambulance and NHS trusts.

"Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patient details in the normal way which is creating a massive backlog and has the potential for chaos," she said, though "emergency and life-threatening call outs appear to be unaffected".

Meanwhile, police forces in England and Wales - including the Metropolitan Police, Greater Manchester Police and Police Scotland - have said online forms may be affected. They are urging people to call them about any time-critical by non-emergency matters.
Downing Street said it was looking to get a "full picture" of the the extent of the outage's effect on government services.
In England, the Local Government Association warned that some services may be disrupted but plans were in place to ensure people "continue to receive the support they need".
Because the outage affects key organisational and communication platforms that are integrated, many other workplaces have been affected.
That has included schools, where teachers, office staff and parents have all had to navigate being unable to access key resources on calendars, emails and internal cloud servers.

One head teacher at a primary school near Newcastle said safeguarding systems had also been affected, meaning staff were having to report concerns in person instead of logging them, while another in Cheshire said his had been forced to delay sending out termly school reports.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2: Trainees in obstetrics and gynaecology are reporting more feelings of overwork and sleep deprivation
Training doctors working on maternity wards are experiencing high rates of burnout which could have a "critical impact" on patients, a regulator is warning.

The General Medical Council (GMC) says the fully qualified doctors, who are still training in obstetrics and gynaecology, are reporting more feelings of overwork and sleep deprivation than similar trainees in any other field of medicine or surgery, and are also more wary of escalating concerns.
Author Adam Kay, who left medicine in 2010 after dealing with a traumatic birth incident, says the report "makes for miserable reading" and says "nothing has been done" to improve workplace culture.
The Department for Health and Social Care said ensuring every maternity unit "meets the highest standards" was a priority.
The GMC analysed figures from its national training survey, which in 2026 was completed by 68% of trainee doctors, which includes registrars, representing almost 52,000 people.

Almost one in three trainee doctors working in obstetrics and gynaecology felt hesitant or apprehensive approaching a senior colleague about a patient, compared with one in five across all specialties
They were also more likely to be at moderate to high risk of burnout - 70% versus 61% across all specialties
One in three said they regularly suffered from sleep deprivation compared to one in five across the wider pool of trainees
Charlie Massey, head of the GMC, said having doctors who feel they cannot speak up, could have a critical impact on patients.
"Creating environments where staff are supported, listened to and feel able to raise concerns is essential."
He told the BBC: "Sadly, when we see when things go wrong, it is it is very often because of failures in terms of culture and leadership."
Adam Kay says he wasn't well supported while working as a doctor
Author Adam Kay says the findings echo his own time as a doctor.
He went on to write This is going to hurt: Secret Diaries of a junior doctor about his experiences, including caring for a mother who delivered a stillborn baby.

"I wasn't particularly well supported after it happened. It was a bit like I said I'd sprained my ankle or something. There was no talk of a debrief. There was no offer of time off or counselling. It's just, you know, get on with it."
He described the GMC report as "pretty miserable reading" and suggested that nothing had changed since he left the profession 16 years ago.
"The doctors working on our labour wards are burnt out, bullied, don't feel like they can report problems upstream. It's upsetting to read."
Aside from a negative work culture, a key problem, Kay suggests, is lack of staffing.

"There are fewer staff on the wards than ever. I can't remember the last time I spoke to a doctor in that specialty who wasn't working out what their plan B was, whether that's going part time, moving to another country, or moving to the pharmaceutical industry.

"It will always be busy and high pressured, but there are things you can affect. You can affect the number of people who are working there and you can affect the culture. You should be able to speak to your boss. You should be able to go and take a break and go for a cup of tea or a wee, and that's not the case at the moment."
Dr Miriam Broughton, 27, is a resident doctor in her second year of training to become an obstetrics and gynaecology consultant.
While the decisions she has to make sometimes keep her awake at night, she says she wouldn't change her job for the world.

"Being there to deliver someone's baby at the best moment of their life is honestly one of the best things you could ever do. And then also working with people through the hardest moments of their lives and being able to support them is just priceless."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98r: Cancer charities and doctors say sunbeds are linked to higher rates of melanoma and other skin cancers
A watchdog has launched a crackdown on misleading sunbed adverts, warning tanning firms they must not claim their beds are safe or can treat medical conditions.

The Committee for Advertising Practice (CAP) said it was issuing a UK-wide enforcement notice to "send a clear message to the industry that advertisers must not downplay the risks associated with sunbed use".
Earlier this year, the BBC identified hundreds of social media videos claiming the beds could boost energy and treat skin conditions or mental health problems.

The Sunbed Association, which represents around half of the UK's tanning salons, said it fully supported action against misleading adverts, but said businesses must still be allowed to demonstrate they operate responsibly.

The CAP, which draws up the UK's advertising rules, said some of the claims being made by companies were potentially harmful and could discourage customers from seeking appropriate medical treatment or advice.
"Sunbeds carry serious health risks, including an increased risk of skin cancer," said the CAP's compliance executive James Burnett.
"Ads shouldn't downplay those risks or present sunbed use as a way to improve health."
Cancer charities and doctors are clear about the risks of using sunbeds - and say the machines are linked to higher rates of melanoma and other skin cancers.
Using a bed before the age of 35 increases the risk of melanoma by 59% later in life, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Young people are by far the biggest sunbed users in the UK - about one in seven 18-to-24-year-olds say they used one in the past year, double the average for all age groups, according to a 2025 YouGov survey.

Rosie Vare, health information manager at Teenage Cancer Trust, said skin cancer was one of the most common forms of the disease in young adults and she welcomed stricter enforcement of the advertising rules.

"We want young people to be properly informed about the risk of sunbed use and we recommend using trusted, regulated sources to find out information such as the NHS , external or cancer charities , external ," she added.
The wider health and beauty sector in the UK is estimated to generate sales of £6.1bn a year, according to market researchers Whito

The CAP said it had identified a series of misleading health claims in sunbed advertising, including suggestions that tanning beds can ease eczema symptoms, improve brain function, reduce inflammation and boost circulation.
Earlier this year, the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), which enforces the CAP code, banned five adverts that claimed sunbeds could help manage conditions including osteoporosis and depression.
The new enforcement notice warns businesses not to make medical claims, promote sunbeds as a source of vitamin D or suggest sunbeds are safe.
Sunbed use is legal and regulated in all parts of the UK, with limits on the strength of the UV light the beds can emit and a ban on under-18s using the devices.

According to the Sunbed Association, its members train staff to screen out high-risk customers with very fair skin and, under its guidelines, no individual should be allowed to buy more than 60 sessions a year.
The organisation's chairman, Gary Lipman, said he would never encourage members to use health claims to promote their products.
He said he has worked with the CAP to ensure the code would not stop members explaining how they comply with regulations.
"We fully support action against misleading advertising. But there is a world of difference between claiming something is risk free and explaining that a business operates responsibly," he said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c617: Consultant doctors in England have called off their two-day strike this month to hold talks with the government.
The walkout was due begin on 25 November at 06:59 GMT, with consultants staffing emergency care only.
This is known as Christmas Day cover and was likely to have a major impact on most routine and elective or planned services.
But the British Medical Association, the trade union for doctors, said it was pausing the action to discuss pay and working conditions with the government.
Consultants – the most senior doctors in hospitals – were given a 3.5% pay increase this year.

But the BMA argues pay has fallen by a quarter over the past 17 years, once inflation is taken into account – although this is using a measure of inflation that tends to be higher than the one favoured by economists.

The union also wants a reduction in the standard working week, from 40 to 35 hours, and higher pay for out-of-hours work, alongside changes to pensions, including greater flexibility over when they can be taken.
Meetings have been taking place over recent months, but the BMA is now entering formal talks with the government's negotiating team. They could start as soon as this week.

In a statement, BMA consultants committee co-chairs Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta said: "We welcome the opportunity to enter formal negotiations with the government and hope this marks a turning point in a dispute that has gone on for far too long.
"We've always said strikes do not need to go ahead as long as the government is willing to genuinely negotiate and now is their chance to do so.
"We have received assurances that there are no constraints on what we discuss in these negotiations, and we look forward to hearing their proposals on both pay and working conditions."
But government sources said giving them a bigger pay rise this year was not on the table because of the state of the public finances and current level of their pay.
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the cancellation of the strike was "welcome news for patients and the wider NHS".
"I had a constructive discussion with the BMA on reforms that could give consultants a stronger voice, greater flexibility and more freedom to innovate, while improving services for patients."
In the strike ballot, 76% of consultants who took part voted in favour of strike action, with just over half of eligible BMA members taking part.
The government says this represents only around one in five consultants employed by the NHS in England voting for strike action, as nearly half are not BMA members.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75: William Murphy had to wait 12 hours before an ambulance arrived at his home
When 85-year-old William Murphy became seriously ill at his home in September, his family expected help to arrive quickly.
Instead, they waited more than 12 hours for an ambulance, despite a new initiative - the Release to Rescue scheme - designed to free up crews to respond to calls more quickly.
"Dad was deteriorating... he couldn't walk," his son Ronnie recalled. By the time William reached hospital, he needed oxygen as his levels were severely low.
William's experience was not an isolated case in Northern Ireland, where patients facing lengthy waits for an ambulance are not uncommon.

The Release to Rescue initiative was introduced this year to ensure a maximum two-hour wait for patients stuck in ambulances outside busy emergency departments - therefore allowing paramedics to get back on the road to help other people, like William.
But more than 2,000 ambulance handovers exceeded the two-hour limit between May and August, the first four full months of the scheme.
The Department of Health said the scheme had delivered "improvements", with more than 6,000 waits of two hours or more in the same period last year.
Ronnie Murphy said his father's health deteriorated while they waited for an ambulance
The Murphy family, from County Down, were told over the phone that the ambulance service was "under pressure" and that a crew would come as soon as possible, according to Ronnie.
"I was concerned - the length of time it was taking and Mum was ringing but they were just saying still the same message," he told BBC News NI.
"Whenever he got into hospital he had to go onto oxygen and his oxygen levels were severely low.
"Had there been another emergency, had my dad taken more seriously ill, where would we have been?"
The Northern Ireland Ambulance Service (NIAS) has apologised to William for the "delay experienced following his 999 call".
"The demand for our services exceeds our capacity to respond in as timely a manner as we would like," it said.
The Release to Rescue protocol had "delivered some benefits", it said - but it accepted that "more focus is required to reduce the turnaround times even further".
Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Evening Extra programme , Health Minister Robbie Butler apologised to William.
"I very much regret and apologise to Mr Murphy for any failure on my part, or our part," Butler said.

"It's deeply regrettable and I know that having spent time in the control centre for Northern Ireland ambulance that the staff are absolutely dedicated and committed to ensuring that we have our resources in the right place at the right time."

Ronnie was unhappy that his father spent almost two days in the Ulster Hospital's emergency department before he was admitted to a ward - but added that he had no complaints about the care he received.
"The floor, the waiting area in the new A&E - every seat was filled," he said.
"There were people sitting on the floors; there were people all sitting everywhere; there were people crying, families in distress."
The Release to Rescue initiative aims to cut ambulance handover times at hospitals
The South Eastern Health Trust said it was "sorry to hear of the experience" Ronnie and his family described.
The health minister said there have been "growing pressures over a number of years", but added that "Release to Rescue in the greater part has been very successful".
He said the programme "still faces challenges", adding that as we face into winter pressures those challenges "ramp up".
"I think it's really important that the work that has been embarked upon, and there are multiple layers to that work, continues," Butler said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6qj: A bar-tailed godwit similar to Phil being fitted with a tracking device
A bird named Phil has astonished conservationists by completing a 6,800-mile (10,900km) round trip from England's east coast to Siberia and back.
Bar-tailed godwits are champion fliers, migrating between Britain and the Arctic, but the precise routes used by individual birds is largely unknown.
Phil was fitted with a tiny solar-powered tracker that recorded his movements throughout the journey.
The data showed he travelled from The Wash , external to the Wadden Sea, along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, before continuing to Siberia.
On his return, he crossed the Arctic Ocean to northern Norway, stopping on three islands before heading back through the Wadden Sea to The Wash.
Scientists say Phil's extraordinary travels highlight the importance of protecting the world's wetlands, which are havens for millions of migratory birds each year.

Dr Nigel Clark, of the conservation charity, The Wash Wader Research Group, said The Wash is the UK's single most important coastal wetland for migratory waders, with spectacular numbers seen in autumn and winter.
"Tracking birds like Phil the Godwit shows us how connected the Wash is with the rest of the flyway," he said.
Jeff Kew, RSPB Coastal Advisor, said many migratory bird species cross borders, depending on a whole network of wetlands along the way.
That's why it's so important to look after these special places."
Bar-tailed godwits are wading birds of similar size to pigeons, but with long bills and legs.

They are regarded as one of nature's long-distance endurance athletes, with one subspecies making the longest known non-stop migration of any bird, flying 8,425 miles (13,559km) from Alaska to New Zealand.
Phil's journey included a handful of stops to rest and refuel.
He will now spend the winter relaxing with thousands of other wading birds at the Snettisham Nature Reserve in Norfolk.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8p3: Special Protection Areas are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew
An investigation has found the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs is failing to protect wild birds.
The Office for Environmental Protection said Daera had not complied with environmental law requiring it to classify and update Special Protection Areas (SPAs).
Environment Minister Andrew Muir said their findings made for "uncomfortable reading".
SPAs are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew and whooper swan, which continue to decline in Northern Ireland.
The OEP said action had not been taken to maintain or restore wild bird populations and their habitats.
The director of RSPB NI, Joanne Sherwood, said the findings were "no surprise" and called for urgent action.
A parallel investigation is looking at the same issues involving Defra and Natural England, and they have also been issued with decision notices.

In Northern Ireland, the OEP's Chief Regulatory Officer Helen Venn acknowledged that "positive steps" had been taken, but added that delays in meeting legal obligations had played a part in the significant decline of wild birds in Northern Ireland.

"SPAs are important for achieving the Executive's commitments in relation to nature, such as the strategic outcome of thriving, resilient and connected nature and wildlife in the Environmental Improvement Plan.
"This is in addition to the Executive's international commitment to protect at least 30% of land and seas for nature's recovery by 2030.

"This is why it is important for Daera to carry out its legal responsibilities in a reasonable timeframe to deliver nature recovery and in relation to the classification and adaptation of SPAs on land."
The agriculture and environment minister Andrew Muir said there was "a moral and legal obligation" to protect wild bird habitats and welcomed continuing engagement between his officials and the OEP.

"The OEP has recognised in their investigation longstanding and concerning failures to implement recommended actions to protect wild bird habitats and populations by successive administrations both in England and Northern Ireland.
"While we have a long way to go to reverse current trends, there are signs of hope and clear examples of nature recovery in action.
"However, the scale of challenge requires greater levels of support from across government to provide the necessary resources and funding to address the nature crisis."
And he said the recently-published Nature Recovery Strategy and the Farming With Nature support package "reinforces" the department's commitment to nature restoration.
Sherwood said the group had been highlighting failing for decades.
"Today's findings from the OEP confirm what conservation organisations have been saying: action has been delayed for far too long.

"The focus must now move to delivery, with the Executive leading the way, and Daera and NIEA being resourced to take urgent action to put these protections in place and help reverse the decline of our most vulnerable bird populations.
The decision notice is the latest step in the OEP's investigation.
It identifies failures and recommends what actions Daera should now take to fix them.
It says Daera has failed to classify and update SPAs, has not put measures in place to protect declining birds, and has not carried out a required review of habitats.
Recommendations include addressing outstanding recommendations "where they remain ecologically relevant" from a review of SPAs, carried out in Northern Ireland in 2001.
Where they cannot be implemented, it says "transparent, ornithological reasons" must be published.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62: Firefighter Steve Williams, pictured here with his widow Jilska, died of a rare lung cancer 14 years after falling into a toxic lagoon
It was a sight which struck terror into the firefighters called to tackle it - a blazing chemical waste lagoon on fire, with barrels exploding into the air.
Steve Williams, then in his 20s, was one of 60 firefighters sent to tackle the burning Llwyneinion lagoon in August 1980, which was sending thick black smoke over a nearby village.
Steve slipped in and, although he was pulled out, his widow thinks what he swallowed may have cost him his life from a rare form of lung cancer aged 39. She said "someone should be held accountable".
Wrexham council, which owns the site, said while it did not meet the legal definition of "contaminated land", it regularly inspected and monitored the area.
It took 60 firefighters about 18 hours to bring the 1980 fire at Llwyneinion lagoon under control
A leading expert in fire chemistry and toxicity said it was difficult to establish a link between firefighters' exposure to chemicals and health issues later in life.
Steve's widow Jilska Williams believes the father-of-two's terminal cancer could have stemmed from the chemicals at the fire at the former toxic waste dump near Wrexham in north Wales.

"It's a definite probability," said the 71-year-old. "They're firemen and they're always running into fires, so you don't know what the long-term effects are going to be - but actually falling into the lake and drinking that fluid, which is full of chemicals. He had a double-whammy, didn't he?"
Steve's family are part of a group which came forward after the BBC documentary Buried with Michael Sheen highlighted Wales' toxic waste legacy.
This is the last family photo of Jilska and Steve Williams, with their children David and Kelly, taken in June 1994, shortly before he was diagnosed with terminal lung cancer
They want surviving firefighters to be tested for deadly carcinogens they fear they were exposed to in the fire at the Llwyneinion lagoon.
Eleven firefighters or their families have told a BBC investigation about concerns the fire could have had an impact on their health.
They said there was an increased number of miscarriages suffered by partners of those who attended the fire in the year after - and also highlighted concerns about rates of cancers since.
Steve followed his dad into the fire service in 1978 and his first posting was in Wrexham, where he was among the first responders to the lagoon fire.
The 1980 fire at a lagoon used as a dumping site for chemicals was fought for two days.
Jilska said he was checked at hospital after falling in, then given a tetanus injection before being sent home.
"What is a tetanus injection going to do for him?" said the retired nurse. "It was a disaster waiting to happen. A time bomb waiting to go off, as far as I'm concerned."
The couple moved to Melbourne in Australia, then in 1994 Steve was diagnosed with stage four cancer - small cell carcinoma , external - and given weeks to live.
Footage from a BBC news report in August 1980 shows the extent of the toxic waste dump fire at the Llwyneinion lagoon
He died three days after the couple's 17th wedding anniversary. Their children were aged six and 10.
The Llwyneinion site was a dumping ground for chemicals suspected to have included cancer-causing polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) from chemical giant Monsanto.

Sheen's Buried programme team found elevated levels of PCBs in soil samples taken in an area open to the public beyond the fenced-off lagoon, as well as at 13 other suspected dumpsites for the firm's toxic waste across the country.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75: The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim.
But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together.

"People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge.
People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years.
But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA).
Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor.

"There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. We don't swim with cuts or anything."
"This summer I got quite poorly," Jenny says, explaining that she'd had diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.
"I'd swum and then within six hours I was unwell. I was poorly for probably about seven to 10 days and it was not nice. I think it was the river that day."
"There are germs everywhere, all over the place. You can catch Covid in Tesco," she says.
The BBC has been investigating whether discharges of treated sewage might be responsible for poor water quality at a bathing site in Taunton.

This summer French Weir Park failed its tests on 13 of the 19 days it was sampled. The BBC analysed data from all four regulators across the UK for 2026 and found French Weir Park's failure rate of 68% was the highest of all the bathing sites.
The regulators look for two types of faecal bacteria – E. coli and intestinal enterococci – that originate either in human or animal guts and can make people ill if ingested.
So where's it coming from at French Weir Park? The local water company Wessex Water says it could have come from wildlife, agriculture, private septic tanks as well as its sewerage works.
We decided to take a closer look to see if we could work out where the truth lies.
Despite the high levels of faecal bacteria and the health warnings, Jenny, Jo and Jo have kept swimming at the bathing site in Taunton
Our wastewater treatment system is built on the assumption that faecal bacteria - from our poo - once discharged into nature will be rapidly diluted and perish.
The bacteria are known to have little impact on wildlife but they can make humans sick if ingested – so the rise in popularity of wild-swimming and testing of bathing sites have increased awareness.
As part of a BBC investigation we analysed the water sampling results from this summer across all the UK's 700 official bathing sites on the coast, in lakes and rivers.
We found that more than 10% of the UK's coastal sites and 37% of its inland sites failed to meet regulators' minimum standards across the summer.
That difference is likely to be because the sea acts as a more effective dispersant and can dilute and kill faecal bacteria quicker than a lake or river.
Of the 11 worst bathing sites in England in 2026, seven were on inland rivers or lakes.
Last year the official advice was not to swim at 12 of the 14 inland river bathing sites in England .

Poor water quality has historically been linked to raw sewage spills. These are much more likely after it has rained. So why, in a summer that was extremely dry, did bacteria levels remain high in so many rivers?
In Taunton the official testing data suggests there has been a constant flow of bacteria entering the river.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c63r: The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".
The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.
The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.
Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".
Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.
In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars
SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.
"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.
The CCC analysis also argued that weakening the targets would lead to a hole in the government's carbon savings that need to be made in order to meet its legally binding climate targets.

The CCC said the ZEV mandate "underpins the largest share of emissions reduction to 2037" in the government's net-zero plan. The climate targets set for 2033-2037 will be missed "without alternative action at the same scale", the CCC argued.
CCC analysis shows surface transport - which includes cars, vans and trucks - remains the country's highest carbon-emitting sector and one of the slowest to decarbonise.
Lord Deben, former CCC chairman, said going against CCC advice would "not be sensible" as it would "cost people money".
He said climate targets were "not random targets" and "if you don't reach them then you put yourselves in really serious danger of having climate change, which we can't handle".

A government spokesperson said: "We remain committed to the phase out of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets. Our consultation on the Mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg: Faizal Shahzad wants to buy several more solar panels to make his home in rural Punjab fully self-sufficient

Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.
But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel.
"In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."
Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.

From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.
People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."

Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.

This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eﬀects.

The big pivot to solar wasn't driven by government policy but by individual Pakistani households. Most people we spoke to said they installed panels to escape soaring electricity prices from an often unreliable national grid.
Electricity tariffs have more than doubled in a few years, says Muhammad Hassan Dajana, industry liaison at Renewables First, while the cost of Chinese solar panels has "decreased by 93%".

"People have just found another way to be able to survive," says Energy Minister Awais Ahmad Leghari. "It's a very healthy thing. We have adapted to the situation. The people have reacted and responded in a very economically viable and efficient manner."
While the solar boom brings clear benefits, particularly for a country that imports huge amounts of fuel, there are worries too.

When people buy less energy from the national grid, fewer customers are left to cover the fixed costs of maintaining it. That can force prices up - which in turn encourages even more people to switch to solar.
Over time, this can lead to a two-tier system in which those who can't afford to buy panels face ever-rising bills, while the national grid becomes an increasing burden on the state.
"You'll have a white elephant in the form of a state-owned enterprise that requires a lot of public funding to just stay afloat," says Dajana.
More and more households are installing solar panels, as seen here in Karachi, but Pakistanis still need energy from the national grid
"In just the past two years, the exodus from the grid has cost the rest of the consumers more than $500 million [£378m] a year," says Leghari. "That's a very big burden."
The government doesn't want to pull people away from solar, he explains, but wants the grid to be more competitive to be able to offer better energy prices.

Private power producers, which feed into the grid, have been heavily criticised inside Pakistan for locking the country into costly, inflexible contracts. Producers themselves point to broader structural problems like poor grid maintenance as contributing to higher bills. Leghari says the government has renegotiated most of the contracts and is now focused on making the grid more efficient with better storage, less waste and more innovation.
