https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm89: The legal action against Natural Resources Wales landed in the High Court
River campaigners are taking on Wales' environmental regulator in the High Court over what they believe is a "regulatory gap" that risks pollution from poultry farms in two rivers.

River Action UK has accused Natural Resources Wales (NRW) of not doing enough to assess or address any risk to local rivers and and other water bodies when plans for three farms in Powys were approved last year.
It follows years of debate over the alleged impact of chicken farming on rivers such as the Wye and Severn - in an area dubbed the UK's "poultry capital" .
NRW said it would be inappropriate to comment ahead of the court case, but that it would "participate fully in the legal process".
The case is about plans to increase the capacity of three Powys farms by a combined 336,900 chickens, bringing the total to 522,000.
Two of the farms, Rhosddu and Llanshay, are in the River Severn catchment while Neuadd Isaf is in the River Wye catchment.
Campaigners said the Severn was showing "signs of strain" with regular algal blooms, brown algae smothering the riverbed.
The three poultry units in Powys are located within river catchments including the River Wye
Campaigners' concerns have centred around the birds' manure becoming a pollutant when it is spread on fields and leaches into rivers.
Nutrient-rich agricultural run-off can contribute to algal blooms, turning rivers green and smothering wildlife.
Following a consultation, NRW approved permit variations in November 2025, allowing the three poultry units to expand.
Rather than keep and spread the manure on site, the farms' operators said they would export it for use or processing elsewhere.

River Action argued NRW wrongly concluded it had no legal power under the Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016 to assess the potential environmental impacts of this off-site manure management, or to take action to prevent or mitigate pollution arising from it.
Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, argues there is a "regulatory gap" in the management of off-site manure
Campaigners set up a chicken-themed protest outside the High Court hearing in Llandrindod Wells on Tuesday.

"River Action will argue that Natural Resources Wales has the power to address and assess the impact of that manure on the environment and, as the specialist regulator, should be lawfully deciding how to use that power when operating the permitting regime," said Julia Eriksen, of solicitors Leigh Day, representing River Action.
The organisation insisted NRW could put controls on the farm's permit to reduce or remove the risk of manure causing pollution.
Campaigners believe the birds' manure will spread on fields and into rivers, causing harm

Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, said NRW "decided that it didn't have the power to look at what would happen when a lot of the manure would go offsite" when the plans were approved in 2025.
"That matters because more chickens means more muck, and that needs to go somewhere and someone has to deal with it," she said.
"So this case is all about making NRW realise that it does have the power to deal with it."

An NRW spokesperson said: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment on matters that are before the court. We will continue to participate fully in the legal process and await the court's determination."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly: Watch: William and Catherine walk green carpet in Mumbai for Earthshot Prize
The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.
Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.
One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.
The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.
They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.
He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".
Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.
The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.
"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."
William and Catherine talk with guests during the awards ceremony in Mumbai
The royal couple also spoke to those performing, which included Take That
There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-Free World; and Fix Our Climate.
Five winners were chosen from a list of 15 finalists who attended Tuesday's awards ceremony.

Protect and Restore Nature: Bhutan, the country that helps to protect the water security of 1.6 billion people across South Asia and has a national nature coalition that aims to revive forests and rivers by restoring 50,000 hectares of damaged land

Build a Waste-Free World: PFAS-Free France, a national campaign that helped secure landmark legislation banning 'forever chemicals' in France by 2030, and hopes to extend the ban to more major countries
Revive Our Oceans: Niue Ocean Wide Trust, the Pacific island's scheme that has safeguarded marine life by investing in conservation to fund the long-term protection of its vast waters

Clean Our Air: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a scheme rolling out up to one million electric rickshaws across India with the aim to drasitically cut one of the world's largest sources of on-road air pollution
Fix Our Climate: Ørsted, a global energy company that has cut its direct carbon emissions by more than 98% by transforming from being highly coal-intensive to a leader in offshore wind
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr5y: The contaminated Mobuoy dump is thought to cover more than 100 acres of land
More than £160m is needed to clean up and maintain one of Europe's largest illegal landfill sites, government officials have said.
The contaminated Mobuoy dump at Campsie in County Londonderry, discovered and shut down in 2013, was used to bury thousands of tonnes of rubbish at a site spanning more than 100 acres.
Last year, two businessmen were jailed for their part in the operation.
Northern Ireland's Environment Minister Andrew Muir said his department had now received an updated cost estimate of £161m for the clean-up over a 30-year period.
Muir described what happened at Mobuoy as "an absolute scandal" and said "the community rightly expects and deserves remediation of the site".
He is now seeking a meeting with the Finance Minister John O'Dowd to discuss how the work will be paid for - with funding from Westminster a possibility.
Once the finances are agreed, they will work towards appointing a contractor.
Andrew Muir says it could take a generation to clean up the Mobuoy dump in County Londonderry
Investigations indicate an estimated 1.6m tonnes of waste was present at the site and 627,000 tonnes of that was believed to have been dumped illegally.
The Mobuoy site is beside the River Faughan, which supplies a significant proportion of Derry's drinking water but officials have not found any contamination to it.
The area of polluted ground stretches to about 100 acres, or the equivalent of about 65-70 football pitches.
"This is a complicated project, as you'll understand, given the complexity of the site," Muir told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Tuesday, .
The minister said he took environmental protection very seriously and would continue to push for the establishment of an independent environmental protection agency.
"One of the massive lessons that needs to be learned from the Mobuoy site is the need for stronger environmental protections, so people have confidence that our environment is being looked after."
The site, located on the outskirts of the city, is a former recycling plant
Muir said the next assembly election was fast approaching in May, so he understood there might be some concerns about the potential costs involved.

One of the UK's largest oil refinery operators has been ordered to pay £873,473 after breaching environmental permit limits nearly 500 times over three years.

The Environment Agency (EA) said the Stanlow refinery in Ellesmere Port, Cheshire, exceeded wastewater discharge limits at least 489 times between 2018 and 2020. Essar Oil (UK) Limited pleaded guilty to 12 charges in March .
Essar Oil, which trades as EET Fuels, was fined £800,000 and ordered to pay £73,473 in costs at Warrington Magistrates' Court.
EET Fuels said it regretted the "historic incidents" and had invested more than £24m to improve environmental performance.
Ten charges related to wastewater discharges containing oil, suspended solids and chemicals, including cyanide, into Thornton Brook, the River Gowy and the Manchester Ship Canal.
The Manchester Ship Canal runs for 36 miles from Eastham in Wirral to Salford
In February 2019, between 15 and 20 tonnes of a chemical leaked into the ship canal after a vent was left open and a written procedure was not followed.
A month later, a contractor's vehicle ruptured an effluent pipe. During repairs, about 15 tonnes of partially treated sewage entered Thornton Brook, which leads to the protected Mersey Estuary.
Environment Agency officers reported a sheen of oil on local waterways, while vegetation downstream of the refinery's discharge point was blackened by oil in January 2020.

The company was fined £80,000 for each of the 10 offences, with no additional penalty for the two 2019 incidents. Three breaches from 2022 and 2023 were taken into consideration without further punishment.
Nigel Glasgow, the Environment Agency's area environment manager, said the case showed "a repeated failure to comply" with permit conditions.
An EET Fuels spokesperson said: "We take our environmental responsibilities extremely seriously and regret these historic incidents."

The company said its investment included rerouting wastewater to United Utilities' Ellesmere Port treatment works, resulting in "a significant improvement in environmental performance", including fewer discharges and reduced freshwater use.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly: The baby rhino was born after its mother was pregnant for 15 months
The moment a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros took its first steps at a zoo has been captured on video.
The video shows 19-year-old mother Asha with her newborn calf at their enclosure after Asha had been pregnant for 15 months.
Keepers said both rhinos were in good health and the birth was an important step in the conservation of the threatened species.
Tom Garland from the rhino team at Chester Zoo said the calf was the fourth born to Asha and father Beni, who died earlier this year following a short and sudden illness.
"It's always exciting to welcome a new calf and Asha has been a brilliant mum to all her youngsters," he said.
"Every birth is important for the future of this species and it's wonderful to see another healthy arrival."
The greater one-horned rhinoceros species is under threat of extinction

The species was driven to near-extinction in the early 1900s by habitat loss and trophy hunting and remains vulnerable to extinction with around 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos living in the wetlands, forests and grasslands of India and Nepal.
The calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding programme that helps to maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos in human care.
Conservation scientist John O'Hanlan said supporting Asha's 15-month pregnancy had been "really exciting".
"She's one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is important in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population," he said.
The birth is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding programme

Mark Brayshaw, Head of Mammals at Chester Zoo, said in addition to safeguarding the genetics of the species, Asha and her calf could also help millions of zoo visitors understand the value of conservation.

"Greater one-horned rhinos are much better protected in the wild than they once were, but many of them are concentrated within one national park in India, which makes them vulnerable to illness and environmental changes," he said.

Consumer NZ says when it comes to Black Friday sales , you can trust some retailers more than others.
The pre-Christmas shopping season has become a key feature of many New Zealand retailers' promotional plans.
Consumer said it had been tracking the sales price of products and found that Briscoes were the easiest to trust as genuine sales while Noel Leeming's were hard to gauge.
It tracked the prices of 13 products over 12 weeks at five retailers: Briscoes, Farmers, Harvey Norman, JB Hi-Fi and Noel Leeming.
To qualify as a sale, the Fair Trading Act says a special must be a genuine opportunity to buy a product at a discount, which is only available for a short period of time.
Consumer said Briscoes was best at clearly communicating a genuine opportunity to save. The prices repeatedly returned to full price between
promotions, and Briscoes used less promotional language and labelling than the other stores.

"Everyone knows Briscoes has a lot of sales. What sets Briscoes apart from the other stores is that prices don't fluctuate as much. Our analysis showed products are either on sale, generally at up to 50 percent off their highest price, or they're full price," said Rebecca Styles, research lead at Consumer.
"Given the regularity of sales at Briscoes, you should feel sorry for yourself if you pay full price for a product there."
But she said it was still sometimes possible to find things cheaper than their "on sale" Briscoes price.
"Across the three months we were tracking the sales, the best price Briscoes offered for a specific Ninja air fryer was $125. The same product at Noel Leeming dropped to $97."
Consumer ranked Farmers second because it said some of its promotional language could be confusing to some consumers.

"At Farmers, we observed a regular pattern of a product being on sale for a few weeks before returning to full price. But its use of a 'great price' label let the store down. The term 'great price' didn't reliably indicate a low price," Styles said.
For example, a top-loader washing machine at Farmers was labelled as a "great price" every week for 12 weeks. That "great price" varied from $1248 to $1669.
JB Hi-Fi was third because its use of promotional language sometimes did not correlate with an item being a good deal.

"A Breville Barista Express was 'on sale' for $600, and a week later it was a 'red hot deal' at $698. It was also a 'red hot deal' at $848. Some of these descriptions ceased to be meaningful," Styles said.

The highest price of the coffee machine at JB Hi-Fi was $999. So while the "specials" were all an opportunity to save, the widespread use of hyperbole made it hard to distinguish the level of discount.
Consumer said Harvey Norman had made its promotional language easier to understand but it was still promoting prices that were not particularly good deals.
That included a handheld garment steamer that was $34 cheaper when it wasn't labelled a "hot deal" and an air fryer that was $10 cheaper when it wasn't a "birthday deal" or "hot deal".
Consumer said Noel Leeming was being too heavy handed with advertising that promised a "price smash", "epic deals", "massive sellout" and "mega deals".
"It's impossible to know which promotional label represents the biggest opportunity to save," she said.

Convicted double murderer Scott Watson has been denied parole for the sixth time, but the parole board indicated he has taken steps toward his release.
At the conclusion of Thursday's hearing, the board told Watson they believed he still posed an undue risk to the community after 27 years in prison.
But board member Alan Hackney told Watson the board agreed he was in the re-integrative phase of his sentence, and scheduled another hearing for July 2027.
The 55-year old has spent 27 years behind bars after being found guilty in 1999 of the murders of Ben Smart and Olivia Hope.
The Blenheim friends, aged 21 and 17, were last seen stepping off a water taxi onto a stranger's yacht in Endeavour Inlet the early hours of 1 January, 1998.
Their bodies have never been found . Police said Watson murdered the pair, dumping the bodies in Cook Strait. Watson has consistently denied the charges and still maintains his innocence.
Watson made several unsuccessful applications to appeal his convictions before a 2017 bid for a royal pardon was granted, with the case heard by the Court of Appeal in 2024.

That court turned down the appeal last year , finding no miscarriage of justice in relation to forensic evidence from Watson's yacht or in the identification of Watson by water taxi skipper Guy Wallace.
In March, the Supreme Court of New Zealand granted Watson leave to appeal the decision in part - specifically on the issue of Wallace's identification of Watson in a police photo montage.
The decision in the case, which was heard last month, has been reserved.
A parole bid in January was declined after the board viewed CCTV footage from 2024 of Watson attacking another prisoner, though his lawyer said the incident had been misrepresented.

At the time, the board suggested Watson undertake further treatment to address his attitudes to violence and women, have an Autism Spectrum Disorder assessment and work on his safety plan before reappearing.
Members of the board and a representative of the Department of Corrections acknowledged the progress Watson had made at Thursday's hearing, congratulating him on the work he had put in.
Watson, wearing a grey tracksuit, thanked his support people and the parole board, and expressed empathy for the victims.
His lawyer Kerry Cook KC told the board Watson was not an undue risk to the community, referencing three safeguards that would support his re-integration.

Parole conditions, the stability of the family address Watson would be paroled to, and "the protective effect of his steadfast maintenance of his innocence, which gives him every reason to stay beyond reproach" would ensure his release could be managed safely, Cook said.
Updated specialist reports including a neuropsychological assessment and risk evaluation found Watson posed a low-to-moderate risk of further violence, Cook said.
The reports noted Watson's reserved emotional presentation reflected long-term institutionalisation rather than anti-social intent.
Watson had a minimum security classification, had tested negative for drugs, had a carefully constructed safety plan and was "respectful and compliant with staff instructions", he said.

The long-time owner of a popular Wellington nightclub says Courtenay Place is "the worst it's ever been", with venues sitting empty and locals staying away.
Dakota, a cowboy-themed bar loved by university students for its famed mechanical bull, closed earlier this month after 14 years in business.
It joins a number of other nightclubs and restaurants that have closed in the area - The Garden Hotel, Red Square, BL3, and Siglo.
"It's really quiet ... it's a shame that we're the capital city and for a Friday night, it's grim," Dakota owner Jose Ubiaga said.
"The amount of closed venues that are floating around - it's the worst it's ever been."
Dakota bar had its licence suspended earlier this year, after it was caught selling alcohol to a 16-year-old for the second time.
Ubiaga told RNZ the closure had nothing to do with the licence suspensions.
"It was a battle to get my licence, and I've been having to battle for the last five years.
"It was tiring and hard work and I did it myself, I never hired a lawyer."
Ubiaga said the cost to run his nightclub in Wellington had become too high, particularly when it came to alcohol licence fees and rent prices.
Wellington City Council charged between about $870 and $9360 annually for an alcohol licence, including an application fee.
Ubiaga said just one in four people who did come out to the bar were buying drinks anyway. He said he'd always have a soft spot for the venue.
"It's been great, it was a good bar. It was probably my favourite one that I'd done over the last 23 years."
In September, The Ministry for Regulation recommended alcohol licensing fees across the country should be recalibrated under its annual Hospitality Regulatory Review.
The review recommended that one nationwide licensing system should be created, rather than individual councils setting their own fees.
Hospitality chief executive Kristy Phillips backed this change.
"Courtenay Place, like lots of areas around New Zealand, is going through its challenges.
"We definitely see a place for licensing council regulators to be working hand in hand with the industry to basically reset some of the settings to increase the viability of business."
Phillips said the review made clear an inconsistency of licensing and compliance costs throughout the country.
The Reading Cinemas building is being redeveloped, after sitting empty for many years.

Development group Te Aro Hā has begun revamping heritage buildings in and around Courtenay Place, using the council's Heritage Resilience and Regeneration Fund, starting with restaurant Winner Winner's venue.
Spokesperson Miranda Richardson said new vendors were joining the area beyond the nightlife scene - lighting store ECC, boutique hostel Drifter, and a sauna studio called Hā.
She said the development group wanted to shift the area from a nightlife spot to a place people would come to throughout the whole day - an "18-hour neighbourhood".
The redevelopment of the Reading Cinemas building , expected to open in late 2027, was promising for the street.
"These are the types of spaces that, once you get them buzzing and busy again, new things start to barnacle off them," Richardson said.

Many New Zealanders do not understand how relationship property rules apply to de facto relationships, and it can make break-ups complicated and expensive , one legal expert says.

Lauren Milne, JustFund's New Zealand director of family law, said its data showed almost 80 percent of people could not correctly identify when relationship property equal-sharing rules generally applied to de facto couples.
JustFund offers legal loans to help with family law fees, divorce, and relationship property separation.

Under New Zealand law, relationship property is usually evenly shared when a couple has been together three years, but there can be exceptions to that timeframe when there is a child or a partner has made significant contributions.

The law says a relationship is de facto when people are over 18, live together and are not married or in a civil union. But " living together " does not always require that the couple only has one home that they share. The law says to determine whether people are living together as a couple, things that should be taken into account are whether or not a sexual relationship exists, the degree of financial interdependence and support, the ownership and use of property, the degree and commitment of a couple to a shared life, the care and support of children and the performance of household duties, as well as the reputation of the relationship.
Audio player for " Susan Edmunds on the cost of misunderstanding de facto rules " removed for printing
JustFund found 43.6 percent of people thought the threshold for the law to take effect was two years not three, and another 20.4 percent were not sure when the rules applied at all.
"A lot of people think it's a two-year rule, some say five years, some say they didn't know it applied at all, of course it doesn't actually even just come down to specific time frames," Milne said.
"There are a number of factors that the courts will look at as well that I think are probably not very widely known in New Zealand."
She said people might not realise that it did not matter who brought property into a relationship when it came to dividing it.

"What we will often see is one party owning a property, the other party moves in and it becomes the family home, and after that three-year period there is this presumption that that then becomes relationship property and there is a 50-50 sharing available. But there are actually a number of factors that a court will look at.

"Living together is a very strong indicator, but living together full-time isn't strictly mandatory to find a de facto relationship. Other factors that the court will look at are whether the parties have an intimate or sexual relationship.

"This doesn't even need to be exclusive. They'll look at financial dependence or interdependence, whether the bank accounts are shared. They will look at whether one party is contributing to the other party's property, care and support of children, household duties, and it's really this overall mutual commitment to a shared life."

One of the country's most expensive schools can continue to exclude students from activities like cross country races and sports coaching unless they stump up nearly $11,000 for the privilege.

A district court case challenging Whanganui Collegiate's optional fee for day students wanting access to property and services provided by its owner, the Whanganui College Board, but not covered by its integration agreement with the government has been struck out.
The decision at the end of October followed an Ombudsman's investigation that concluded the practice did not appear to be unlawful.

The man who brought the court case , Craig Sinclair, told RNZ he worried the two decisions opened the way for other schools to make access to certain facilities and activities contingent on paying a fee.

The school's website said students who purchased access to the non-integrated facilities had access to boarding houses, "prep spaces during the School day, tutor support, pastoral care support from the Health Centre, Housemasters, Residential Masters and Matrons, along with House supervision during timetabled breaks".

"As an Anglican school, it contributes to our faith and chaplaincy. NIFfDS students participate in all Inter-House sport and cultural competitions, co-curricular activities such as the House Swimming, Athletics and Cross Country events, House Music, Tikanga and other School-wide House activities," the site said.

Sinclair contended that the fee should be optional because some of the activities provided via the charge formed part of collegiate's special character and he said took place during regular school time.
He said students who did not pay the fee were excluded from a large part of school life and other integrated schools asked families for a donation to cover similar costs.
"They're operating a school that's half state, half private," he said.

"The ministry at the moment have got an opinion that what Whanganui Collegiate School is offering is a very high-quality, expensive, after-school programme and that is a load of nonsense because the cross-country is during school time, the swimming sports is during school time, quite a few of these things are during school time."
He said he was worried the decisions opened the way for other schools to charge high prices for activities that many people would consider standard.

"I can go around New Zealand and educate all the state schools and state integrated schools that you can do it this way and charge parents fees and it will lead to the erosion of section 33 the Education and Training Act where all New Zealanders when they turn five till the 31st of December after their 19th birthday receive a free education," he said.
A long-time campaigner against the high fees and donations charged by some integrated schools, Guy Gifford, made the Ombudsman's complaint.
Gifford said collegiate's practice of charging a fee rather than asking for a donation deprived families of tax credits worth thousands of dollars.
He said regulations were designed to prevent integrated schools offering an environment superior to regular state schools.

The New Zealand Association for the Teaching of English says it has concerns about the quality of the new NCEA English exam students hit by a technical glitch last week can opt to resit given the condensed timeframe.
The New Zealand Qualifications Authority (NZQA) is preparing a new NCEA level 2 English exam in just a week and a half, so students can resit it following major technical problems last week.
NZQA has apologised for the disruption and said students affected by the online glitches would be able to opt to sit the new test on 4 December - but only on paper.
NZQA chief executive Christian Hawkesby said the process of creating an exam usually took about 18 months, but would now be done in about 10 days.
He said the unusual step was necessary because analysis showed students had been adversely affected by the disruption.
New Zealand Association for the Teaching of English president Pip Tinning told Morning Report it was likely NZQA had back-up exam options already in place but the process was not clear.
"But if they have back-ups in place and they're now using those, are those the rejects that they didn't want to use in the first place?
"I would hope that they were scrambling on Thursday and started that process immediately just in case that was the option."
Following a second, but different, technical problem this week NZQA announced an independent review.
Tinning said it was necessary for the review to be transparent, with all recommendations acted on, in order to restore her faith in the online testing system.

"It'd be interesting to know whether it was a capacity issue, whether there was some technical glitch that meant it went down when we had too many students on, just knowing what on earth is going on would be really helpful."
She feared teachers across the board would give up on online exams.
"I think we're about to have ... a whole group of educators who are just going to be, 'I can't trust your system anymore'.
"Do we have to go back to pen and paper in 2027? In 2027, can you imagine."
She told Morning Report that the NCEA level 2 English exam was high stakes because some students would require it for University Entrance literacy.
Tinning said although offering a resit was probably the only option in this situation it put a lot of unnecessary pressure on students.
NZQA chief executive Christian Hawkesby said preparations for the additional Level 2 English exam on 4 December were being taken with "both pace and care".

"The exam will use the paper which was in development for 2027. This has been prepared through our usual process, and we are moving through the final steps so that it will be available for students," he said in a statement.
Schools need to inform NZQA about the expected number of entries by next Wednesday.

"We are aware this is a tight turnaround from yesterday's announcement, but it is important that there is enough time to ensure sufficient exam rooms and support staff available for the number of students who might be expected," Hawkesby said.
He added NZQA has undertaken to conduct a full independent review. The key findings will be released publicly.

Auckland University of Technology dean of law school Khylee Quince said the figures needed to be seen as part of a bigger picture which has Māori disproportinately represented in prosecutions and convictions in all offence categories.
"Drug use and possession and drug-related offending is just a smaller picture of that bigger picture."
Quince said there were three main conclusions she could draw:
She said 1000 people were charged and convicted solely for possession of meth or cannabis, 15 were sent to prison and 11 of those people were Māori.
Those people had not been arrested for other offences so had probably been randomly stopped by police when they were in vehicles or on the street.
The 2019 amendment to try and cut down the number of people prosecuted was "clearly not working".
"That tells us that police have either not been properly informed or trained as to how to interpret and apply those legal obligations."
Police were not meant to prosecute unless it was in the public interest and must consider a health-related response instead.
"The police should be policing differently and there's clear evidence that they aren't."
While she welcomed diversity within the police force, she questioned how officers were being trained and equipped to be robust in their interpretation of the law.
"This tells us something about what we should be doing at police college and the way in which these people are supported to do their job in the community."
Dave Burnside is the lived experience leader at Odyssey Trust, an addiction treatment service based in Auckland.
"Particularly when most of the world is turning to a health not handcuffs approach and recognising the futility of criminalising drug use particularly and possession," he said.
Burnside had his own experience with the system, where minor cannabis charges led him on a downward spiral to other offending and prison time.
"It gave me a criminal record, it affected my opportunities in terms of employment, travel, education and other things," he said.

Police received a report at 7.40pm on Thursday about a member of the public being threatened with a gun on Whitewood Cresent in West Melton.
Some police officers who responded were armed as a precaution.
The Eagle helicopter was also deployed to assist, senior sergeant Mike Jackson earlier said.
Online flight trackers showed the chopper circling above the town and returning towards Christchurch Airport shortly before 9.30pm.

Community groups in the Northern Mariana Islands have questioned the timing of United States Air Force consultations on expanded military training, with the first meeting held just two days before the territory's gubernatorial runoff election.

Representatives of Right to Democracy, From Luta, For Luta, and Our Common Wealth 670 raised concerns at Wednesday's meeting on Saipan, saying the election campaign and limited public comment period could restrict meaningful participation.
Right to Democracy co-founder Adi Martinez-Roman said her organisation rescheduled a community dialogue to allow residents to attend.
"Also, there is an election process that is going on in the community. So, people are distracted, but understandably so," she said.
Martinez-Roman also questioned whether the consultation format, which required residents to examine information displays and approach military officials individually, was sufficiently accessible.
Right to Democracy's Zeno Camacho Deleon Guerrero Jr said people in the US territories deserved meaningful consultation on federal decisions affecting their lands, waters, and skies.
He also raised concerns about the cumulative effects of military expansion and other proposed developments, including deep-sea mining.
From Luta, For Luta organiser Catherine Atalig said her group opposed further militarisation, particularly because of potential environmental impacts on Rota.
"We're here to express our refusal of the hyper-militarization of our islands," she said.
The US Air Force announced plans to prepare an environmental impact statement for aircraft training and exercises at four airfields across the three islands.
Pacific Air Forces spokesperson Technical Sergeant Soo Kim said he could not comment on the timing of the meeting during the runoff campaign but encouraged residents to submit their concerns.

Lieutenant Colonel Onnie Retkofski said the proposal would support changing Air Force training requirements across the Pacific, with military exercises coordinated to avoid disrupting commercial flights.
She said she could not comment on whether the consultation period would be extended.

Three protesters also delivered statements during the meeting at Pacific Islands Club Saipan, raising concerns about aircraft noise, fuel contamination, threatened wildlife, and the environmental pressures facing islands recovering from successive typhoons.
The Air Force proposes expanded training at four airfields across Saipan, Tinian, and Rota, with up to 1,200 fixed-wing aircraft operations and 320 helicopter operations annually at each location.
Our Common Wealth 670 has called for the initial 30-day consultation period to be extended to at least 60 days.

Similar public consultations were scheduled for Thursday at Tinian Western Lodge and Saturday at the Rota Mayor's Office, allowing residents of both islands to raise concerns directly with Air Force representatives.
Written submissions close on 29 November, while the final environmental impact statement is expected in 2028.
No final decision has been made on the proposed military activities.

More needs to be done so people reaching retirement don't shift all their money to cash or conservative investments, KiwiSaver providers say.
The Financial Markets Authority has said more advice should be given to people who are turning 65 and reaching the age at which they are eligible to access their KiwiSaver accounts.
Ana-Marie Lockyer, chief executive of Pie Funds, said the industry needed to do "much more" to help people make their savings last through retirement.

"Turning 65 shouldn't automatically mean cashing out or moving everything into conservative investments. We don't see a massive spike of age-related withdrawals from KiwiSaver but I think there's still a lack of awareness that you can remain invested in KiwiSaver after 65, with no requirement to withdraw your money. For many New Zealanders, that makes good financial sense, particularly when retirement could last another 20 or 30 years, and will be important with growing nest eggs."
She said there was growing interest in a goals-based approach, where people thought about their money in terms of different buckets.

"Money needed in the short term might be held in cash or more conservative investments, while savings they won't need for another 10 or 20 years can remain invested for growth. The right balance depends on individual circumstances, income needs, and risk tolerance .

"As an industry, we've focused heavily on helping people accumulate retirement savings, but arguably also need to support how they manage and draw down those savings. This includes helping people understand the risks of being too conservative too early, particularly with inflation and increasing life expectancy.

"Good financial advice can make a real difference, and these conversations should start well before 65. Ultimately, KiwiSaver shouldn't just be about getting New Zealanders to retirement. It should be about helping them achieve financial security throughout retirement."
Robyn Conway, general manager of wealth at Fisher Funds, said many people had been conditioned to think they needed to withdraw all their money when they had access to it.

"But with most people living up to another 20-plus years, it's important to keep your money working hard for you while also being able to withdraw money to top up your income or for big ticket items."
She said people could use the bucket method and keep the second and third buckets working over time to refill the cash bucket as required.
Murray Harris, head of KiwiSaver at Milford, said it would become increasingly important that people were getting good advice and guidance about making their money last.
"That will include remaining invested for most of the money, be that in KiwiSaver or an investment fund, rather than putting it all in the bank and going backwards versus inflation.

"Most of our members turning 65 do remain in their KiwiSaver account, although many do review their fund choice and risk appetite. We send our members a series of emails as they approach 65 outlining the options they have with their funds and highlighting the availability of an online tool they can use post age 65 to show them how much they can draw down annually depending on which fund they choose and how long they want the funds to last. They can then set up an automatic payment from their KiwiSaver account to their bank account if they choose to draw down the funds. This tool is proving popular which suggests there is good demand for more of these services. Speaking with a financial adviser would also be a very good idea at this stage of life."

Why have rents started increasing , even while house prices keep falling ?
ANZ senior economist Matthew Galt said new tenancy rents were now about 1 percent higher than a year ago, and the change in the market had been seen across the country.
While growth of 1 percent was still significantly below normal levels of rent inflation, it was a change from the past year or two in which rents had generally fallen.
Galt said rents were rising as the economy slowly improved but the significant increase in housing stock, both for sale and rent, would reduce the scale of the increases.

"Rents tend to follow the economic cycle closely. They're driven by things like population growth and employment growth and wage growth. The gradual economic recovery we've seen over the last year has started to flow through into a fairly modest increase in rental demand."
He said rental demand growth tended to correspond closely with total aggregate wages paid across the economy.

"This captures both individuals' wage growth and population growth. This has tracked changes in rents closely over time. It began lifting last year shortly before new tenancy rents turned around. The improvement over the past year has reflected a combination of population growth, employment growth, and modest wage growth. The improvement in the economic cycle has clearly had an impact on rents - but the lift has been relatively muted, consistent with the economic recovery being gradual so far."
Galt said the data clearly showed that wages, and what tenants were able to pay, was the biggest driver of rents.

"When wages rise or more people enter jobs or the population grows, that's when you tend to see rents rise. When landlord costs go up, for example, if interest rates rise and landlord's interest expenses rise, only a very small fraction of that tends to be passed through to rents in practice. And that's because landlords, by and large, are already charging as much as the market is willing and able to pay. And just because landlord costs have gone up doesn't mean they can immediately pass those costs on to tenants."
He said, if the economy continued to improve as ANZ expected, rents would probably rise between 1 percent and 3 percent over the coming year.

"Recent high numbers of first-home buyers are unlikely to have impacted the balance of supply and demand in the rental market. To a reasonable approximation, when a household buys their first home, this just shuffles existing households between houses, rather than changing the total number of households and houses in existence."
Galt said a key difference was that higher interest rates had little impact on rent but put pressure on house prices.

"The improvement in the economy that's supporting rents will also be supporting house prices to some degree, but house prices are impacted by a wider range of factors. In particular, house prices are very sensitive to interest rates, and higher interest rates are now weighing on prices. Election uncertainty and low expectations of capital gains are also likely to have been weighing.
"Are rents also impacted by higher interest rates? Some landlords may try to pass higher costs through to rents, but research finds very little pass-through in practice.

Documents show some staff at a youth justice facility were too scared to report worrying behaviour such as colleagues engaging in sexual behaviour with teenagers.
The details are contained in a debrief as part of a "reset" staff training plan put in place in September last year to improve standards at Korowai Manaaki at Wiri, in south Auckland.
It said Oranga Tamariki (OT) staff were hesitant about reporting poor practice, often due to fear of being seen as "snitching."
Since then, the ministry says the reset plan has improved safety, culture and workforce stability.
The head of Youth Justice Services for OT says there is a "significant programme of wider work underway in our residences, which is seeing positive results".
Poor practice described in the debrief from last year also included ignoring contraband being brought into the facility and favouritism.
"There was a perception that kaimahi who do raise issues are not adequately supported," the debrief read.
The document also said kaimahi spoke about being sent into a "war zone" with little protection or support from OT when they were hurt.
There was also frustration with the regular changes in senior leadership and increasing wariness about the effectiveness of reset training.
Another training debrief noted a lack of trust in senior leadership was consistently raised, attributed to frequent changes in those leading the site.
"Many kaimahi expressed cynicism that practice resets have been attempted before" without leading to sustained change.
The absence of "visible consequences" for poor practice was highlighted frequently as well.
It comes after RNZ reported a punch-up between a staff member and a young person took place in September - a year after a "reset plan" was undertaken at the facility to lift standards.
Oranga Tamariki told RNZ last year's 12-week Reset Plan at Korowai Manaaki was a standalone project.

"Internal reporting showed it resulted in measurable improvements at the residence, across safety, culture, and workforce stability," Dean Winter, Oranga Tamariki, DCE Youth Justice Services and Residential Care said.
He said there was a "significant programme of wider work underway in our residences, which is seeing positive results".

There was also ongoing training and change programmes underway, which set clear expectations to staff about their procedures, agreements and code of conduct. There were also other initiatives underway that enable universal searches on entry to reduce harmful items.
As well, OT said their residences have channels in place for kaimahi to speak up with any concerns they might have and for leadership teams to address these.

When asked about the concerns raised in the training debrief, Minister for Children Karen Chhour referred to earlier comments about the improved training programme being an important step towards better practice, "but I acknowledge that it will take time to embed".
"This training is just one part of Oranga Tamariki's efforts to fix long-standing issues stemming from a previous lack of standard operating procedures and adequate training at these facilities.
"I am confident that once these efforts are fully implemented, they will significantly improve the safety of young people and staff."
A report from OT to the Minister in December 2025 had also acknowledged "while some harm is still occurring on site, practice in managing complex dynamics and reducing risk of violence has improved."

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/voyager-1: NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. It passed the milestone on 18 November 2026.

A light-day is how far light travels in a whole day. Voyager 1 is now about 26 billion kilometres away, more than four times as far as Pluto is from the Sun. That means a signal sent from Earth takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft.

Voyager 1 is about the size of a small car and launched from Florida, in the United States, on 5 September 1977. Along the way, it photographed Jupiter, Saturn and Titan, which is Saturn’s largest moon.

In 1990, it took 64 pictures that together made the first “family portrait” of the solar system. In 2012, it moved beyond the reach of the Sun’s magnetic field and into interstellar space, which is the space between stars.
The spacecraft has lasted far longer than anyone expected, but eight of its 10 science instruments no longer work. Within the next ten years, scientists may receive its very last signal.
For now, Voyager 1 is still sending back information about space beyond our solar system. Next year, it and its twin, Voyager 2, will both have been in space for 50 years.
Pānui: Kua tae a Voyager 1 ki te tawhiti o te light-day kotahi i Papatūānuku
Ko te waka ātea a NASA, a Voyager 1, te mea tuatahi i hangaia e te tangata kua tae ki te tawhiti o te light-day kotahi i Papatūānuku. I tae atu ia ki taua tohu i te 18 o Noema 2026.

Ko te light-day te tawhiti e haere ai te marama i te roanga o te rā katoa. Kei te tata ki te 26 piriona kiromita te tawhiti o Voyager 1 i tēnei wā, neke atu i te whā whakareatanga o te tawhiti o Pluto i te Rā. Nō reira, e 24 hāora te roa kia tae atu tētahi tohu i tukuna mai i Papatūānuku ki te waka ātea.

He rite te rahi o Voyager 1 ki tētahi motukā iti, ā, i whakarewaina mai i Florida, i Amerika, i te 5 o Hepetema 1977. I tōna haerenga, i tango whakaahua ia o Hupita, o Hatana, me Titan, te marama nui rawa o Hatana.

I te tau 1990, i tango ia i ngā whakaahua e 64, ā, i hanga ngātahi ai te “whakaahua whānau” tuatahi o te pūnaha o te Rā. I te tau 2012, i haere ia ki tua atu o te papa autō o te Rā, ki te ātea i waenganui i ngā whetū.

Kua roa ake te ora o te waka ātea i tā te katoa i whakaaro ai, engari kua kore e mahi ngā taputapu pūtaiao e waru o ōna taputapu e 10. I roto i ngā tau tekau e heke mai nei, tērā pea ka whiwhi ngā kaipūtaiao i tōna tohu whakamutunga rawa.
I tēnei wā, kei te tuku mai tonu a Voyager 1 i ngā mōhiohio mō te ātea i tua atu o tō tātou pūnaha o te Rā. Ā tērā tau, ka 50 tau a ia me tōna māhanga, a Voyager 2, e noho ana i te ātea.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/leaders-o: US President Donald Trump, China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin are holding their first-ever three-way meeting. The talks are taking place on 19 November 2026 in Shenzhen, China.
The meeting is happening alongside Apec, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. Apec is a big gathering of countries in the region that meet to talk about trade.
No one knows exactly what the leaders will discuss in private, but there are some big issues affecting all three countries.
The war between the US and Israel on one side and Iran on the other has hurt economies around the world. China is the biggest buyer of Iran’s oil.
The US and China are also racing to become the world leader in artificial intelligence, or AI.

Russia has been more cut off from other countries since it invaded Ukraine in 2022. Experts think a breakthrough on ending that war is unlikely. European leaders, and especially Ukraine, are worried about talks that don’t include anyone from Ukraine.

Vladimir Putin has led Russia since 1999, sometimes as President and sometimes as Prime Minister. Donald Trump began his second term as US President in 2025, after first serving from 2017 to 2021. Xi Jinping has been China’s leader since 2012.
BBC China Correspondent Laura Bicker said the meeting is a chance for President Xi to show China as a bridge between big countries.
Details of what the three leaders agree on, if anything, are expected once the talks are over.
Pānui: Ka hui ngā kaiārahi o Amerika, Haina me Rūhia mō te wā tuatahi

Kei te hui tahi te Perehitini o Amerika, a Donald Trump, te Perehitini o Haina, a Xi Jinping, me te Perehitini o Rūhia, a Vladimir Putin, mō te wā tuatahi rawa. Kei te tū te hui i te 19 o Noema 2026 ki Shenzhen, i Haina.
Kei te tū te hui i te taha o Apec, arā, te Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. He hui nui a Apec mā ngā whenua o tēnei rohe hei kōrero mō te hokohoko.
Kāore tētahi e mōhio pū ki ngā kōrero a ngā kaiārahi i tā rātou hui tūmataiti, engari he take nui kei te pā ki ngā whenua e toru.
Kua raru ngā ōhanga huri noa i te ao i te pakanga i waenganui i Amerika me Iharaira i tētahi taha, me Iran i tērā taha. Ko Haina te kaihoko nui rawa o te hinu o Iran.
Kei te whakataetae hoki a Amerika rāua ko Haina kia noho ko rātou te kaiārahi o te ao mō te atamai hangahanga, arā, te AI.

Kua noho mokemoke ake a Rūhia i ētahi atu whenua mai i tana whakaeke i Ūkareina i te tau 2022. E whakaaro ana ngā tohunga kāore pea e kitea he huarahi hou hei whakamutu i taua pakanga. Kei te māharahara ngā kaiārahi o Ūropi, otirā a Ūkareina, mō ngā hui kāore he tangata nō Ūkareina e uru ana.

Kua ārahi a Vladimir Putin i a Rūhia mai i te tau 1999, i ētahi wā hei Perehitini, i ētahi wā hei Pirimia. I tīmata a Donald Trump i tana wāhanga tuarua hei Perehitini o Amerika i te tau 2025, i muri i tana wāhanga tuatahi mai i te tau 2017 ki te tau 2021. Ko Xi Jinping te kaiārahi o Haina mai i te tau 2012.
E ai ki te kaikawe kōrero o te BBC i Haina, a Laura Bicker, he whai wāhitanga tēnei hui mā te Perehitini Xi ki te whakaatu i a Haina hei arawhiti i waenganui i ngā whenua nunui.
Ā muri i te hui, ka mōhiotia ngā mea i whakaaetia e ngā kaiārahi e toru, mēnā he mea i whakaaetia.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/study-fin: If your cat keeps meowing at you, it might be asking for a hand. A new study from the University of São Paulo in Brazil has found that cats use meows, along with eye contact, to ask their owners for help.

The researchers visited 38 cats in their own homes. Each cat was given a treat trapped inside a small plastic box with holes in it, so it could see and smell the snack but couldn’t get it out by itself.

When a person was in the room, the cats meowed 85 times, compared with just 20 times when they were alone. That’s about four times as many. Overall, the cats were 16 times more likely to meow when a human was around.

With no person nearby, the cats mostly stayed quiet, stood still and stared at the door. When a person was there, the cats meowed while looking straight at them, and kept glancing back and forth between the human and the box.
The researchers also found that feral cats meow much less than pet cats. Feral cats live on their own and don’t belong to anyone.
The study was published in the journal Animal Behaviour . It says meowing isn’t just a cat showing how it feels. It plays a “communicative role”, which means it’s a way for cats to talk to people.
So next time your cat meows and stares at you, it may simply be asking for a little help.

Mēnā ka miau tonu tō ngeru ki a koe, tērā pea kei te tono āwhina ia. Kua kitea e tētahi rangahau hou nā te University of São Paulo i Parīhi, ka miau ngā ngeru, ka titiro hoki ki ngā kanohi, hei tono āwhina i ō rātou rangatira.

I toro atu ngā kairangahau ki ngā ngeru e 38 i ō rātou ake kāinga. I hoatu he kai reka ki ia ngeru, kua mau i roto i tētahi pouaka kirihou iti he kōputaputa ōna. Ka kite, ka hongi te ngeru i te kai, engari kāore e taea e ia anake te tango mai.

I te wā he tangata i roto i te rūma, e 85 ngā miau a ngā ngeru, engari e 20 noa iho i te wā i a rātou anake. Tata ki te whā whakareatanga te nui ake. Ina whakarāpopotohia, e 16 whakareatanga te nui ake o te tūponotanga ka miau ngā ngeru mēnā he tangata kei reira.

Ki te kore he tangata i te taha, i noho wahangū te nuinga o ngā ngeru, i tū mārie, ā, i titiro atu ki te kūaha. I te wā he tangata kei reira, i miau ngā ngeru me te titiro tika atu ki taua tangata, ā, i huri haere tō rātou titiro i waenganui i te tangata me te pouaka.
I kitea anō e ngā kairangahau he iti ake te miau a ngā ngeru mohoao i tō ngā ngeru mōkai. Ka noho motuhake ngā ngeru mohoao, ehara i te mōkai a tētahi.

I tāngia te rangahau ki te hautaka Animal Behaviour . E ai ki te rangahau, ehara te miau i te whakaatu noa a te ngeru i ōna kare-ā-roto. He “tūranga whakawhitiwhiti kōrero” tōna, arā, he huarahi mā ngā ngeru hei kōrero ki te tangata.
Nō reira, ā muri ake nei, ina miau tō ngeru me te titiro mai ki a koe, tērā pea kei te tono āwhina noa iho ia.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/bee-swarm: Auckland is seeing about twice as many bee swarms as usual this spring, with local beekeepers getting up to 10 calls for help a day.
Ken Brown, president of the Auckland Beekeepers Club, said the milder winter was the reason. He said the swarms had started about four weeks earlier than normal.
A swarm happens when a hive gets too crowded. The bees raise a new queen, and the old queen flies off with up to half the colony to start a new home somewhere else.
Brown said this is natural and “a sign of a good, strong, healthy hive”. In one backyard, thousands of bees turned up at once.

Phil Lester, a biology professor at Victoria University, said bees had been breeding well and growing their numbers. He said bees are important because they pollinate many of the crops we grow for food.
Swarms are being spotted all over New Zealand, and experts think swarming season could last until January.
Brown said swarms are not much of a risk to people, even if they can be a surprise to see in the city.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/darth-vad: A lightsaber used by Darth Vader in two Star Wars films has sold for US$4.875 million, making it the most expensive Star Wars item ever sold at auction.
The lightsaber was used in The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi. It appeared in the famous duel in Cloud City, where Darth Vader tells Luke Skywalker, “I am your father.”
It was sold by Heritage Auctions in the United States, at an event called the Ultimate Star Wars Auction. In an auction, people bid against each other, and whoever offers the most money wins.
The sale beat the old record, set in July, when Luke Skywalker’s lightsaber sold for US$3.75 million. That means Vader’s lightsaber went for more than US$1 million extra.
The auction also included 27 other lightsabers, along with items from all nine main Star Wars films and other movies and TV shows.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/des-bucki: New Zealand Football has confirmed Des Buckingham as the new head coach of the All Whites, New Zealand’s men’s football team, starting on 1 July 2027 and continuing through to the 2030 FIFA World Cup.
Buckingham will also lead the New Zealand Men’s Under-23 team as they aim to qualify for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.

He is not new to New Zealand football. Buckingham lived and worked here for seven years, including as an assistant coach with the All Whites and head coach of the Men’s Under-23 side. In 2019, he guided that team to qualification for the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and to New Zealand’s first-ever Pacific Games football gold medal.
That same year, he led the Men’s Under-20 team to the country’s highest-ever finish at a men’s FIFA World Cup tournament, including a record 5-0 win over Honduras.

Since then, Buckingham has coached around the world, most recently as head coach of Al-Kholood in Saudi Arabia. He also led English club Oxford United into the Championship division for the first time in 25 years.
New Zealand Football chief executive Andrew Pragnell said the appointment was a big moment for the sport.
“I’m incredibly proud to announce Des as the new All Whites Coach,” Pragnell said. “This is huge for New Zealand Football and the future success of both NZF and the All Whites.”
Fans will have to wait until next July to see Buckingham take charge.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/new-parki: From December, visitors will have to pay to park at some of New Zealand’s most popular outdoor spots, as the Department of Conservation (DOC) rolls out paid parking more widely.
Sites getting paid car parks include Goat Island north of Auckland, the Tasman Glacier, Kura Tāwhiti/Castle Hill, the Routeburn Divide, and the Kepler Track control gates, among others.

At most of these places, the cost will be $2.50 for every half hour, or $20 for the whole day. At Goat Island, the first 10 minutes are free for quick drop-offs and pick-ups, and there is a separate $15 daily rate over winter.

People who live nearby can buy a $10 annual permit instead, which covers unlimited parking all year for up to two vehicles. School groups, DOC volunteers and community groups will be able to apply for an exemption.
The new fees follow a trial that started in the South Island earlier this year, at places like Punakaiki’s Pancake Rocks, Franz Josef and Aoraki Mount Cook.
David Butt, DOC’s director of heritage and visitors, said the money raised, expected to be about $3 million over the next year, would help look after the sites.
“We will use paid parking to generate revenue to contribute to the long-term care of places like Goat Island,” he said.

Cameras will keep track of cars coming in and out, and anyone who doesn’t pay could be issued a $75 breach notice – so if your family is planning a summer trip to one of these spots, it might pay to bring some extra coins.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/robert-pa: British actor Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next James Bond, becoming the seventh actor to play the famous spy in the 64-year-old film series.
Amazon MGM Studios shared the news with a short video clip showing Pattinson, 40, stepping out of the shadows holding a gun, the character’s classic pose.
Pattinson is well known for playing Edward Cullen in the Twilight films, Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter, and the title role in The Batman. He is currently filming the sequel, The Batman Part II.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement.

The new film, known for now simply as “Bond 26,” will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, who also directed the Dune films. “I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond,” Villeneuve said.

Filming is expected to begin next year. It will be the first Bond film made since Amazon bought the MGM film studio in 2022, and the first where the Broccoli family, who have led the franchise for decades, haven’t personally chosen the lead actor.

The Bond films, based on novels by Ian Fleming, have earned more than US$7 billion at the box office since the first film in 1962. Fans will have to wait a while yet to see Pattinson in action as 007.
